article_text:
Edvard Munch once described his famous painting series The Frieze of Life as ‘impressions from the life of the soul’. Through powerful images, Munch explored feelings we all recognise - love, loss, and loneliness in a changing world.

This compelling new exhibition, organised in collaboration with the MUNCH museum, looks at Munch’s ‘soul paintings’ through the lens of cinema and visual storytelling. With unique input from contemporary filmmakers and academics, the exhibition will bring unprecedented insight into his radical tales of identity and desire.

The exhibition includes key works from The Frieze of Life , alongside large-scale paintings, prints, photographs, Munch’s experimental film and rare archival material. By exploring universal themes of passion, pain, and inner turmoil, the show reveals why Munch’s work still feels so relevant in an era shaped by online sharing, self-expression and emotional honesty.

Exhibition organised by Tate Modern in collaboration with MUNCH.

Edvard Munch is presented in the Eyal Ofer Galleries. Supported by Tate Members.

article_text:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

After building massive buzz from its surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival last month, A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is finally here.

The incredibly secretive film was made by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ahead of Holmes’ 11-year prison sentence from her Theranos fraud case. Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited Fielder, Oppenheim and their crew into their home to film, and Fielder even ends up living with the couple 24/7 for full access. The three-hour documentary has a lot to unpack about Holmes, Evans and their bizarre relationship, but we’ve tried to narrow down the most WTF moments below.

So many of the spoilers for “You Can See Everything” have been under heavy protection in the weeks leading up to its release, but we can now dive deep into everything about the movie. The biggest reveal is that Amanda Seyfried returns to play Holmes after her Emmy-winning performance in Hulu’s 2022 limited series “The Dropout.” Fielder recruits her and “Girls” alum Christopher Abbott to play Holmes and Evans in recreations of private conversations between them and Fielder. For fans of Fielder’s HBO series “The Rehearsal,” using stand-ins to reenact moments like that is nothing new, but getting actual A-list celebrities is next-level for the comedian.

In addition to being a documentary about Holmes and Evans’ lives, the movie blurs a line between Fielder as an interviewer and his own evolving relationship with the subjects. It’s nearly impossible to tell when Holmes, a convicted fraudster, is telling the truth, lying or simply is too far removed from reality to distinguish the difference between the two. Evans is also well-versed in deception and manipulation, and he plays a larger role in the film after Holmes’ incarceration.

See some of the most shocking, mind-boggling and WTF moments from “You Can See Everything” below.

Amanda Seyfried Plays Elizabeth Image Credit: Getty Images The most jaw-dropping moment of the documentary — and the most heavily guarded — has to be Seyfried joining the film as herself and also playing Holmes. About halfway through the doc, Fielder recruits Seyfried to get her take on his odd interactions with Holmes, since she won an Emmy for playing the Theranos founder on Hulu’s “The Dropout.” Seyfried’s role in the movie soon snowballs into her getting back into character and re-enacting real conversations that Fielder had with Holmes. Her participation also serves as a way for the actress to mentally unpack and reckon with playing Holmes on TV, which caused many people to think “The Dropout” was more factual than it actually was.

Christopher Abbott Plays Billy Image Credit: Getty Images In another surprise celebrity moment, “East of Eden” and “X-Men” star Abbott plays Evans alongside Seyfried as Holmes. The two actors re-create a meeting that Fielder, Oppenheim and their A24 team had with the real Holmes and Evans before filming began. Abbott then returns later in the doc as they re-enact Fielder’s meeting with Holmes in prison. Abbott and Seyfried had previously starred together in “The Testament of Ann Lee,” which may have been how he was recruited to the film.

The Egg Moment Early in the film, Fielder is interviewing Holmes and Evans as they make breakfast at home. Holmes is whisking eggs and talking to Fielder when Evans abruptly takes the bowl away from his partner and proceeds to whisk the eggs himself. Noticing the brief awkward moment, Fielder asks why Evans did that, and Holmes replies that Evans thinks she doesn’t prepare the eggs the right way and that he can do it quicker. It’s a quick moment but illustrates early on that Evans can be controlling over Holmes’ life, even with minor details.

Billy Goes Full Frontal In an early, bizarre moment, Evans is filmed working out at a gym and then is seen showering completely naked at home. It’s a shocking, uncomfortable scene that alerts audiences that something may be off with Evans. Was it a power play or alpha-male move? Afterwards, he has an awkward moment with Fielder when he walks past the director while wearing just a towel.

Elizabeth Says She’s Never Lied in Her Life Holmes, who was convicted of defrauding Theranos investors, claims she’s never told a lie in her life — not even a little white lie. Fielder grills her about this early in the film, but Holmes can’t think of any fib she’s ever told. It remains a mystery how Holmes is able to completely separate her own version of truth from actual reality, especially after she’s been convicted of fraud.

‘FYI You Can Totally See Everything’ Text The unique title of the doc is never explicitly explained, but it references an odd text from Holmes to Fielder that seems to be sent while she’s out on the beach with Evans. It comes after the couple agrees to let Fielder live with them 24/7 to film the doc, and Holmes writes “fyi you can totally see everything…” The text and its meaning are never brought up by anyone in the film, so it’s unclear if it was an oddly friendly text from Holmes to Fielder or there was some other reason behind it.

Who’s on First? Fielder shows Holmes the famous Abbott and Costello comedy routine to try to get her to acknowledge her confusing, or purposely misleading, language about the failed Theranos technology. In a previous scene, Holmes said the Theranos blood test can work, but that the scientific processes to make it work don’t exist yet — so it cannot currently work but Holmes asserts that it still can. When asked if she finds “Who’s on First?” funny, Holmes says “yes” but can’t articulate what’s funny about it. She can’t see the correlation between it and her own intentionally ambiguous phrasing and starts to tear up; Evans then says that she has her own beautiful view on the world and that’s one of the reasons he loves her.

Billy Interrupts Elizabeth’s Dad In an early contentious moment, Evans interrupts an interview between Fielder and Holmes’ dad where they touch on Holmes’ personal relationships. Holmes’ father had been talking about Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, Holmes’ ex-boyfriend and Theranos COO who was also convicted of fraud. According to Holmes’ dad, Balwani, who’s 19 years older than Holmes, was the real mastermind behind the Theranos case and manipulated the younger founder. When Fielder asks what the father thinks about Evans and Holmes’ relationship, Evans interrupts and asks for the interview to end. When they try to start back up, Evans shuts it down again.

Elizabeth Watches ‘The Dropout’ Image Credit: Courtesy of Hulu After Holmes says she hadn’t seen “The Dropout,” Fielder shows her Hulu’s fictional series starring Amanda Seyfried as the Theranos founder. Holmes and Evans sit in bed, with Fielder nearby watching their reactions, but it proves too challenging and Holmes has to turn the laptop off. Seyfried won an Emmy for playing Holmes in 2022, and the show was nominated for best limited series.

Nathan Offering to Leave So Elizabeth and Billy Can Have Sex Leading up to reporting for prison, Holmes spends her final hours as a free woman with her family…with Fielder awkwardly close by. To give her and Evans some alone time, Fielder offers to leave them alone so they can go have sex one last time. They don’t take him up on it, but they do shower and freshen up before Holmes leaves to begin her sentence.

Nathan’s Prison Gift Before they say their goodbye, Fielder has a gift he wants to give Holmes ahead of her prison stay, but he prefaces it by saying it may be in poor taste. Holmes opens the present and sees that it’s hair dye and sunglasses, which Fielder explains as a joke in case she wanted to escape from prison. Holmes’ parents, who look on silently, are not fans of the present.

Nathan and Elizabeth Say Goodbye Fielder and Holmes have a surprisingly sweet, albeit awkward, goodbye before she heads to prison. They hug and a tearful Holmes tells Fielder that everything is going to be ok, even though she’s the one going to jail for 11 years. They linger and look at each for just a few seconds too long, with the camera zoomed in close, that you wouldn’t be wrong to think that they might’ve nearly kissed had this been a romance movie.

Billy Makes AI Elizabeth In another bizarre choice after Holmes goes to prison, Evans has her body scanned and hires a company to create an lifelike AI version of her. Evans put a large screen in his new house and can interact with the AI Holmes, which replicates her speech.

Billy Asks to Be Paid During the recreation of Fielder and Oppenheim’s off-camera conversation with Holmes and Evans (played by Seyfried and Abbott), it’s revealed that Evans asked to be paid for their participation in the doc while Holmes stepped away. A24 had agreed to pay them, which would’ve severely impacted the credibility of the entire project that was supposed to be an independent look at the couple’s life. Then there’s the question of whether Holmes knew about Evans’ request to be paid. Did she intentionally leave the room while Evans negotiated so she could deny she knew anything about it? Or did Evans go behind her back while she was gone and demand to get paid on his own? In the end, however, it’s revealed that Evans withdrew his request for payment after filming, though no other explanation is given.

Billy Supports Charlie Kirk Seyfried and Fielder confront Evans about whether or not Holmes knew that he had requested to get paid for the doc, and their conversation quickly gets heated. Evans reveals that he’s been posting from Holmes’ verified X account, replying to comments and even trolling people while posing as Holmes online. He also claims that he has power of attorney over Holmes, which shocks and upsets Seyfried. When she speaks up, Evans lashes out at the actress and says that she’s only frustrated because she’d been getting backlash online for her comments about Charlie Kirk, who had been assassinated days prior. Evans then says he had supports Kirk’s beliefs (which should come as no surprise to viewers).

Amanda and Elizabeth Talk on the Phone When Seyfried and Fielder visit Evans, they’re surprised when Holmes happens to call from prison at the same time they come over. Holmes spends most of her two-minute call speaking to Evans and their kids, but then Evans introduces Seyfried, who’s sitting on the couch with them. She and Holmes speak briefly but cordially, though Seyfried is mortified that she’s taking up precious time when Holmes could be talking to her kids. It’s the first, and seemingly only, time the two have ever spoken, since Seyfried hadn’t consulted the Theranos founder before playing her on “The Dropout.”

Billy Says He Can Harm People Fielder pays Evans one more visit after the contentious meeting with him and Seyfried, and things once again don’t go over well. Evans reveals that he’s armed 24/7 for his own safety and says that he knows ways to harm people, which paints him as even more of a villain in the film. He also claims to have a pre-recorded video ready to release publicly if he’s ever killed in a targeted attack.

Billy’s Pets Roaming the House Once Holmes is in prison, Evans moves houses to be closer to visiting her, which also gives him the opportunity to buy several new creepy-crawly pets. According to Vanity Fair , Evans owns a blue Argentine tegu, a corn snake, a curly-haired tarantula, blue death-feigning beetles and two Burmese forest tortoises. The tegu, a large lizard, is seen roaming the house freely while Fielder and Oppenheim film.

Nathan and Elizabeth’s Prison Phone Call After Holmes goes to prison, Fielder tries to get ahold of her to talk on the phone, but Evans tries to block the call. Evans explains that if the prison finds out that Holmes’ phone call is being recorded, she could wind up being punished. At first, Fielder is incredulous and pushes for the call, and finally Holmes comes through and calls him. But instead of hearing the actual audio, Fielder recreates it using Seyfried as Holmes’ stand-in once again.

The Swimming Reveal The movie ends on a quiet reveal: that Holmes and Fielder had gone swimming together earlier while he was staying with her and Evans. It’s not a bombshell moment, but rather one that calls into question how much of Fielder and Holmes’ relationship was a professional one vs. an authentic friendship.

article_text:
シンガポール「ART SG」、2027年版も東南アジアの現代アートに光を当てる「S.E.A. Focus」を併催

東南アジアを代表する アートフェア 「 ART SG 」が、2027年1月に シンガポール で開催される。第5回となる今回は「S.E.A. Focus」を再び併催。タイの作家、ピナリー・サンピタックによる没入型展示など、会場外でも多彩な企画を展開する。

東南アジアを代表する国際 アートフェア 「 ART SG 」が、2027年1月22日から24日まで、 シンガポール のマリーナベイ・サンズで開催される。

第5回となる今回も、 アート・アセンブリー が主催し、 UBS がリードパートナーを務める。参加アーティストや出展ギャラリーは、2026年11月に発表される予定だ。

その全容の発表に先立ち、前回に続いて東南アジアの現代アートに特化した展示・販売イベント「 S.E.A. Focus 」の併催が決定。9回目を迎える同イベントでは、キュレーターのジョン・タンが「Better Worlds（よりよい世界）」をテーマに、技術の進歩や交流の拡大によって変化する現代の暮らしを、東南アジアの作家たちの視点から問い直す。相互の繋がりが深まる世界で、私たちはどのような社会を築き、ともに生きていけるのか。多様な表現を通じて、その可能性を探る。

会場外では、タイのアーティスト、ピナリー・サンピタックとアートスペース・シドニーによる没入型展示を11日間にわたり行う。会場は、かつて米の倉庫として使われていた歴史的建造物「 72-13 」。対話や食事、パフォーマンス、ワークショップ、音楽を通じて、人々が集い、体験を分かち合う場をつくり出す。シドニーとシンガポールを結ぶ3年間の協働プロジェクトの一環で、2028年にはアートスペース・シドニーでの大規模な回顧展へと繋がる。

美術館の作品収集や新進作家への支援も継続する。「SAM ART SG基金」は、国際的な現代アートの収集に25万シンガポールドル（約3100万円）を充て、シンガポール美術館による、第一線で活躍する作家や新進作家の重要作品の取得を支援する。また、UBSが協賛する「ART SG FUTURES賞」では、FUTURESセクターで紹介される優れた新進作家1人に1万米ドル（約158万円）を授与する。

ART SG 会期：2027年1月22日（金）～24日（日）※21日はプレビュー 場所：マリーナベイ・サンズ（10 Bayfront Ave Singapore 018956） 時間：11:00～19:00（22日は12:00～19:00）

title_original: Da Michelangelo Pistoletto a Guglielmo Castelli: il viaggio nell’arte moderna e contemporanea di Aste Bolaffi
editorial_title_zh: 从米开朗琪罗·皮斯托莱托到古列尔莫·卡斯特利：Aste Bolaffi 的现当代艺术之旅
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在都灵，一场横跨一个多世纪艺术史的拍卖会，汇聚了珍稀作品、20世纪艺术大师以及当代艺术中坚。抢先预览精选焦点拍品。文章“从米开朗琪罗·皮斯托莱托到古列尔莫·卡斯特利：现当代艺术之旅……”
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "一位钢琴家、一位吉普赛女郎和花园里的三位公主。在 Aste Bolaffi 定于11月3日在都灵举行的现当代艺术秋季拍卖会上，值得关注的故事有很多，它们跨越了一个多世纪的艺术历程，融合了珍品、大师名作以及展现截然不同探索方向的作品。公众可以在都灵艺术周期间近距离探索这些作品，届时展览将在拍卖开始前开放（10月29日星期四下午 14.00 至 19.00，以及10月30日星期五至11月3日星期二上午 10.00 至 19.00）。", "links": [{"text": "Arte Moderna e Contemporanea", "url": "https://www.astebolaffi.it/it/auction/940?_gl=1*qbcy8x*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..*_ga*MTkyNDcxNDA4Ni4xNzkyMjU3MTM3*_ga_JZGKPCS69V*czE3OTIyNTcxMzYkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTIyNTcxMzYkajYwJGwwJGgxNzc3MjAwNTc0&gclid=CjwKCAjwuczWBhA9EiwAYGgEoUXrBbegFoc6a1SyKm8tyjx04L4-oxY7TONu8udMvA8zPAxJnYnDeBoC_vcQAvD_BwE&gbraid=0AAAAACf8fdzo072fcBUyxIq55z2-hH0fv"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览从版画及限量版本拉开帷幕，其中20世纪的一些重要作品诉说着那个时代的风貌：由乔治·德·基里科（Giorgio de Chirico）和让·谷克都（Jean Cocteau）于1938年创作的作品集《Mythologie》，乔治·莫兰迪（Giorgio Morandi）的一幅珍贵蚀刻版画，以及胡安·米罗（Joan Miró）的大幅版画。此外，还有一小批巴勃罗·皮卡索（Pablo Picasso）的陶瓷作品、萨尔沃（Salvo）由都灵多重画廊（Galleria Multipli）制作的历史名作墓碑《La donnola e la lima》，以及阿利盖罗·博埃蒂（Alighiero Boetti）1978年的书《I mille fiumi più lunghi del mondo》。同时展出的还有包含马蒂斯（Matiz）、贾科梅利（Giacomelli）、丰塔纳（Fontana）、吉尔里（Ghirri）和霍夫尔（Hofer）作品的小型珍贵摄影精选。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/200-869x1024.jpg", "alt": "aste bolaffi", "caption": "MICHELANGELO PISTOLETTO, Pianista, 1962 – 2002. Courtesy: Aste Bolaffi", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，正是在独幅原作中，艺术之旅得以进一步展开，将不同艺术家、不同世代和各种语言串联起来。最先脱颖जु名单中出现的名字之一是维托里奥·泽基（Vittorio Zecchin），展出的是其组画《一千零一夜》（Le mille e una notte）中的十件作品之一，该组画被视为威尼斯自由风格（Liberty）的杰作之一。这件创作于1914年、专为终点站酒店（Hotel Terminus）打造的作品是一幅尺寸为 171 × 169 厘米的布面油画兼金箔作品，估价为 45.000–70.000 欧元。费利切·卡索拉蒂（Felice Casorati）的作品同样重要，此次展出的是一件较为罕见的物件：一个彩绘灯罩。随后是所谓的“都灵六人画派”（Sei di Torino），以一组作品为代表，其中吉吉·切萨（Gigi Chessa）1932年的大型作品《粉红裸体》（Nudo rosa）尤为引人注目，估价 8.000–14.000 欧元。艺术之旅继续展出菲利普·德·皮西斯（Filippo de Pisis）创作于20世纪40年代的两幅《花卉》（Fiori）、马里奥·托齐（Mario Tozzi）1925年的一幅重要花卉画作，以及恩尼奥·莫洛蒂（Ennio Morlotti）20世纪70年代的大幅作品，该作品源自这位艺术家在伦敦马尔伯勒画廊（Galleria Marlborough）举办的著名展览。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/zecchin.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "VITTORIO ZECCHIN Tre principesse nel giardino (Le mille e una notte), 1914 Courtesy: Aste Bolaffi", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雷纳托·古图索（Renato Guttuso）也出现在 Aste Bolaffi 的精选拍品中，目录中包含他的两件极具代表性的作品：1948年的油画《玛古塔街的朋友们》（Amici di via Margutta），以及一幅大型裸体画。在估价最高之列的作品中，还包括恩里科·卡斯特拉尼（Enrico Castellani）2005年的《白色表面》（Superficie bianca），这是一件 100 × 80 厘米的布面丙烯作品，标价 140.000–170.000 欧元；以及马里奥·斯基法诺（Mario Schifano）1979–80年的《无题》（Senza titolo），这是一件 150 × 200 厘米的布面瓷漆与粉彩作品，估价为 60.000–100.000 欧元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/castellani-1.jpg", "alt": "aste bolaffi", "caption": "ENRICO CASTELLANI Superficie bianca, 2005 Courtesy: Aste Bolaffi", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "接下来是拍卖中最珍贵的拍品之一：米开朗琪罗·皮斯托莱托（Michelangelo Pistoletto）。他的《钢琴家》（Pianista），创作于 1962–2002 年，是一幅镜面抛光不锈钢丝网印刷作品，为孤品，尺寸为 148 × 125 厘米。估价为 600.000–800.000 欧元。该作品的核心是艺术家的一项基础研究：图像、反光表面与观者在场之间的关系。在理想距离不远处，还有雷纳德（Reynaud）1967年的混合材料组装作品《Mur 807》，长达三米，具有重要的博物馆收藏价值，估价为 28.000–36.000 欧元。雕塑也占据了广阔空间，涵盖桑德罗·基亚（Sandro Chia）、阿古斯丁·卡尔德纳斯（Agustín Cárdenas）、皮耶罗·吉拉尔迪（Piero Gilardi）等艺术家的作品，其中还包括萨尔沃创作的唯一一件青铜作品《圣乔治与龙》（San Giorgio e il drago），估价 10.000–15.000 欧元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/martini-819x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "ARTURO MARTINI LA ZINGARA (La buona fortuna) 1933 -1934 Grès, esemplare da stampo, foggiatura a colaggio. 208,00 x 50,00 x 50,00 cm Courtesy:Aste Bolaffi", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在精选的特别拍品中，我们不得不提阿图罗·马蒂尼（Arturo Martini）的《吉普赛女郎（好运气）》（La Zingara (La buona fortuna)），材质为炻器（grès），模制件，注浆成型，尺寸为 208 × 50 × 50 厘米，创作于1933年至1934年之间。其历史始于一个大型石膏雕像，是通过与实业家马通（Mathon）合作开发并在1935年罗马第二届四年展（Quadriennale di Roma）上展出的。将一个身高超过两米的形象转化为炻器的技术复杂性，促使马蒂尼不断对模型和模具进行干预，直至达到最终成果。根据作品全集目录（catalogo ragionato），该系列原本应仅包含六件作品。如今人们已知的仅有三件。令这件拍卖拍品的故事更加意味深长的是它的来源：它曾属于多梅尼科·卡拉切尼（Domenico Caraceni），他在1947年直接从马蒂尼手中购得此件作品，并将其保存在米兰的展厅中展示，直至展厅关闭。它的估价是多少？60.000–100.000 欧元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "都灵的当代艺术在更年轻一代艺术家的作品中也占有一席之地，汇聚了一大批艺术家，其中包含古列尔莫·卡斯特利（Guglielmo Castelli）2011年的大型双联画《事物的重量的可变性》（La variabilità del peso delle cose），估价 40.000–60.000 欧元。这一最后的环节将人们的视线拉回当下，强调了与 article_text:
Un pianista, una zingara e tre principesse in un giardino. Nell’asta autunnale di Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Aste Bolaffi, in programma il 3 novembre a Torino, le storie da seguire sono molte e attraversano oltre un secolo di arte, tra rarità, grandi nomi e opere che raccontano ricerche molto diverse. Il pubblico potrà scoprirle dal vivo durante la settimana dell’arte torinese, quando l’esposizione aprirà le porte prima della vendita (giovedì 29 ottobre, dalle ore 14.00 alle 19.00 e da venerdì 30 ottobre a martedì 3 novembre, dalle ore 10.00 alle 19.00).

Si comincia con i multipli e le edizioni, dove il Novecento si racconta con alcune presenze di rilievo: il portfolio Mythologie , realizzato da Giorgio de Chirico e Jean Cocteau nel 1938, una rara acquaforte di Giorgio Morandi e una stampa di grande formato di Joan Miró . Ci sono poi un piccolo nucleo di ceramiche di Pablo Picasso, la storica lapide La donnola e la lima di Salvo, prodotta dalla Galleria Multipli di Torino, e il libro di Alighiero Boetti I mille fiumi più lunghi del mondo , del 1978. Ma anche una piccola e preziosa selezione fotografica con opere di Matiz, Giacomelli, Fontana, Ghirri e Hofer.

È però tra le opere uniche che il percorso si allarga ulteriormente, mettendo in fila artisti, generazioni e linguaggi. Tra i primi nomi a emergere troviamo Vittorio Zecchin , con una delle dieci opere del ciclo Le mille e una notte , considerato tra i capolavori del Liberty veneziano. Realizzata per l’Hotel Terminus nel 1914, l’opera è un olio e oro su tela di 171 × 169 centimetri, con una stima di 45.000–70.000 euro. Importante anche il lavoro di Felice Casorati, presente con un oggetto meno consueto: un paralume dipinto. E poi i cosiddetti Sei di Torino, rappresentati da un gruppo di opere nel quale spicca il grande Nudo rosa di Gigi Chessa, del 1932, stimato 8.000–14.000 euro. Il percorso prosegue con due Fiori di Filippo de Pisis degli anni Quaranta, un importante dipinto floreale di Mario Tozzi del 1925 e un grande Ennio Morlotti degli anni Settanta, proveniente dalla celebre mostra londinese dell’artista alla Galleria Marlborough.

Presente nella selezione di Aste Bolaffi anche Renato Guttuso, in catalogo con due lavori particolarmente significativi: Amici di via Margutta , tela del 1948, e un grande nudo. Tra le opere con le stime più alte figurano poi la Superficie bianca di Enrico Castellani del 2005, acrilico su tela di 100 × 80 centimetri, proposta a 140.000–170.000 euro, e lo Senza titolo di Mario Schifano del 1979–80, smalto e pastello su tela di 150 × 200 centimetri, con una stima di 60.000–100.000 euro.

Ed ecco uno dei lotti più preziosi dell’asta: Michelangelo Pistoletto. Il suo Pianista , datato 1962–2002, è una serigrafia su acciaio inox lucidato a specchio, esemplare unico, di 148 × 125 centimetri. La stima è di 600.000–800.000 euro. Al centro dell’opera c’è una delle ricerche fondamentali dell’artista: il rapporto tra immagine, superficie riflettente e presenza dello spettatore. Poco distante, idealmente, si colloca anche Mur 807 di Reynaud, assemblaggio di materiali misti del 1967, lungo tre metri e di importante interesse museale, con una stima di 28.000–36.000 euro. Largo spazio anche alla scultura, con lavori di artisti come Sandro Chia, Agustín Cárdenas, Piero Gilardi e anche San Giorgio e il drago , l’unico bronzo realizzato da Salvo, stimato 10.000–15.000 euro.

Tra i lotti speciali della selezione menzioniamo Arturo Martini con La Zingara (La buona fortuna) , in grès, esemplare da stampo, foggiatura a colaggio, di 208 × 50 × 50 cm, realizzata tra il 1933 e il 1934. La sua storia comincia con una grande figura in gesso, sviluppata attraverso la collaborazione con l’industriale Mathon e presentata alla II Quadriennale di Roma del 1935. La complessità tecnica di tradurre nel grès una figura alta oltre due metri spinse Martini a intervenire sul modello e sugli stampi fino al risultato definitivo. Secondo il catalogo ragionato, la serie doveva comprendere soltanto sei esemplari. Oggi ne sono conosciuti tre. A rendere ancora più significativa la storia di quello proposto in asta è la provenienza: appartenne a Domenico Caraceni, che lo acquistò direttamente da Martini nel 1947 e lo conservò esposto nel suo showroom milanese fino alla chiusura. La sua stima? 60.000–100.000 euro.

Il contemporaneo torinese trova spazio anche nelle opere delle generazioni più recenti, con un folto gruppo di artisti e il grande dittico di Guglielmo Castelli La variabilità del peso delle cose , del 2011, stimato 40.000–60.000 euro. Un ultimo passaggio che riporta il percorso al presente, sottolineando la vicinanza con la fiera Artissima, prima dell’appuntamento con l’asta del 3 novembre.
excerpt_original: A Torino, una vendita che attraversa oltre un secolo di arte, tra rarità, grandi maestri del Novecento e protagonisti del contemporaneo. Sguardo in anteprima ai top lot della selezione L'articolo Da Michelangelo Pistoletto a Guglielmo Castelli: il viaggio nell’arte moderna e…

article_text:
Three scenes in “Nocturne” nearly knocked me out of my chair: two from excitement, one from exasperation. For a bit of fun, read on and guess which scene inspired which reaction. Or I hope it’s fun, at least, because the dour “Nocturne” is only fun for die-hard fans of the genre — and its cast.

The first stand-out scene will arrive at a different time for every viewer, but for me, it’s shortly after onscreen text identifies the setting as “Fairhaven, Pennsylvania.” That’s when the buzzer goes off, the one that formed in critics’ minds after “Mare of Easttown” and “Task” helped popularize the sound of Delaware County. Now, any show set in the Keystone State — especially a crime show — starts on high alert for lowly accents. And “Nocturne” does not disappoint.

“What are yoo doing here?” Jonah ( Liev Schreiber ) asks his surrogate daughter, Saga (Zazie Beetz), when she shows up to tell the retired cop that his last case — the case that “broke him” (Beetz doesn’t use an accent, so she says her O’s sans inflection) — is active again. One of two missing kids has been found. The clock is ticking to find the other. The cops already called in the feds (specifically, Poorna Jagannathan’s zero-fucks special agent in charge), but they don’t know what Jonah does! “I know yoo suffered, and yoor life was ohver ,” Ida (Chrissy Metz) tells Jonah, begging him to look for her missing kids one… last… time.

So he does! Of course he does. The man is living in a cabin with a giant murder board on the wall, hiking the woods with the faintest hope he’ll stumble across the siblings he was assigned to find oh so many years ago. If that’s not enough evidence that Jonah is haunted, he’s also building a treehouse for his own absent family, who Saga says won’t be back. What happened to them, and why Jonah remains obsessed with this one unsolved case, are details that get slowly dripped out, like in every other sad-dad detective show that stretches a movie-length premise over 10 hourlong episodes.

But hearing that sweet murder-durder voice spring ferth from Ray Donovan is, quite frankly, werth the price of admission for those of us holding an outsized appreciation for actors attempting difficult regional dialects . To be honest, there could be more. Beetz, despite her character growing up in the area, uses her regular voice, perhaps because Saga is an undercover FBI agent who needs to live with a less telling, more neutral intonation. Or perhaps because Beetz is already unconvincing as an undercover FBI agent, introduced via a poorly staged drug bust that hangs the actor out to dry, long before she struggles to match Stephen Graham ‘s serial-killer freak.

Ah yes, there’s a serial killer. The missing kids tie back to Jurek Walter, played by the “Adolescence” Emmy winner with an accent. In the rare instances he speaks, that’s quite fun: a quiet mix of carefully considered words metered out in whispered spurts and soft, equally sporadic vowel sounds. As the Hannibal Lecter type — a brilliant, terrifying killer whose positioning behind bars does little to dissuade our detectives from believing he’s still actively offing people out in the world — Graham doesn’t overdo it. His archvillain, who likes to bury people alive almost as much as he likes psychologically manipulating folks into self-harm, channels his sinister vibes with steady stares imbued with confidence. He likes to show off how much he knows about strangers through observation alone, and then uses those same skills to lure them into his devious plans.

But I digress. “Nocturne” does little to distinguish itself from the oft-copied “Silence of the Lambs” dynamic. Jonah and Jurek share only a handful of brief scenes together through the seven episodes screened for critics, and their moments together feel less electric than perfunctory. Co-showrunners John Hlavin and Rowan Joffé give their actors room to play, but within the bounds of a faux-prestige crime thriller (based on the Swedish novel “The Sandman” by Lars Kepler). Vivid locations ( go birds ), a solemn tone (so dark, so serious), and a talented cast are as capital-B Big as “Nocturne” gets.

At least, so far: The last episode screened for critics finally puts a few clarifying cards on the table, and those major reveals are both clichéd and annoying. I shan’t spoil them here, but how “Nocturne’s” mystery starts to resolve itself betrays the creeping, detailed investigation that makes up a bulk of the story by settling for the easiest and most obvious explanations possible. Astute viewers will likely spot warning signs much sooner, when characters make unearned assumptions to move things along, or when all-too-convenient mistakes occur to string out necessary questions for another few hours.

“Nocturne” relies on its premium-streaming trappings to gloss over these glitches, and depending on your love for the dirty crime drama they’re polishing, they may be an acceptable price to pay for such pleasures as my third-and-final dumbfounding delight: Bill Camp , who plays Fairhaven police chief Dave Ellison, and Ken Leung, as some FBI big-wig, in the same scene! Together! Camp and Leung! The dynamic duo you didn’t know you needed! Better still, there’s reason to believe they’ll share multiple scenes together, as Leung doesn’t appear until the seventh episode, and Camp is in the whole damn show!

Herein lies the not-so-secret sauce behind well-cast genre fare (shout-out to casting director Avy Kaufman): If you hire invested, eminently watchable actors, they can make tired tropes sing. Sure, it’s far more exciting to see Leung sink his teeth into a layered, complex, and specific role like he has on “Industry,” but in a few short seconds here, as the big-city suit trying to flex on a small-town cop, he can still snap you back to attention.

Your drifting focus picks up on a sly note of sarcasm when he questions the locals’ unique methodology. Your drooping eyes fixate on his calculated gaze as it darts around the office before landing, again and again, on the supposed colleague he’s blatantly interrogating. His physical presence, aided subtly by his refined houndstooth overcoat and matching gray buzzcut, clashes with the unkempt cop before him — which, it must be said, only makes it funnier when Camp presents his bulging black eye, shaggy crop of hair, and stubbly, unamused face directly to Leung’s sharp, clean, superior officer, as if to say, “Do you really think your fancy clothes and bossy attitude can intimidate me ?” And Leung wordlessly responds, “I don’t care.”

The scene is a classic jurisdictional dispute, plain and simple. But Camp and Leung bring just enough personal vehemence and lived-in decision-making to make this clash more memorable than 99 percent of the 99 million that preceded it. That’s why you hire them. That’s why you hire the actor Richard Price hired to root Stephen King’s mystical boogeyman story in an irrefutable reality in “The Outsider.” That’s why you hire the actor Chris Mundy and Damon Lindelof hired to ground the shape-shifting alien mystery in “Lanterns.” That’s why you hire the actor Jonathan Demme hired to help legitimize the crazy mind-control plot in “The Manchurian Candidate.” (OK, I guess Denzel helped a bit, too.)

As The New York Times’ chief TV critic James Poniewozick likes to say , you can’t turn a bad show into a good show simply by hiring good actors. “Nocturne” proves that as much as any single show can. But for anyone in the tank for a grim cop vs. killer story, it’s just a little bit better than it should be thanks to the people in front of the camera. These folks know how to get a scene on its feet — and how to make an audience follow suit.

Grade: C

“Nocturne” premieres Friday, October 30 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 10) on December 25.

article_text:
These are paintings that would feel right at home on the walls of someone’s Florida condominium

When an abstract artist offers an instruction for interpreting their work, the prescription can encourage a one-dimensional reading. Such is the case with the painter Agata Bogacka, who invites her audience to consider her oeuvre as a critique of politics in her native Poland, which has in her lifetime – she was born in 1976 – pivoted from communist totalitarianism to free-market democracy. Its society, however, is still riven by ideological debates, not least surrounding LGBTQ rights. Bogacka paints sweeping, frequently pastel-toned strokes with an exceptionally wide brush that lends her (otherwise blank) canvases a distinct character – saturated colour to one side of the stroke; mere traces at the other. These gradations, the artist insists, represent a metaphor for the political spectrum and its vagaries. But without her direction, you’d be unlikely to guess this.

Interactionship (all works 2026) presents a suite of 10 paintings carrying loaded series titles – Disagreement, Declarations, Annexation, to cite just a few, appended with numbers. We’re left in no doubt that Bogacka – who identifies as queer – cleaves to the progressive side of Poland’s identity debate. The exhibition is bookended by a pair of paintings titled Equality Dream (respectively numbers 11 and 12 from an assumedly larger sequence) that co-opt the rainbow-hued LGBTQ flag into an abstract-expressionist-derived schema. The first dissects the emblem, splitting it into separate rainbow blocks that overlap only at the corners of their opposing right angles; the flag’s yellow stripe is rendered in a custard-like hue that divides the otherwise bare, unprimed canvas into clear halves. The colours in the second descend in a narrow, centrally oriented vertical zip, their intensity fading into an expanse of blankness. These pieces are perhaps the most successful here, retaining an ambiguity rather than projecting an explicit message.

Elsewhere, a symmetrical diptych – Avoidants 7 & 8 – sees Bogacka’s work branch into, or at least towards, the territory of conceptual sculpture. A diagonal, downward-moving swath of Barbie-pink lines the lefthand canvas, its intensity fading into blankness as your eyes shift right; this gesture is almost mirrored by the opposite panel. Read generously, the void at the diptych’s centre and the cleavage between the two paintings might hint towards an absence of political vision; and an unbridgeable gap between ideological poles. Declarations 14 and 16 , meanwhile, give us rectangular forms again defined by gradation, and roughly the size and shape of A4 paper sheets, appearing to drift over expanses of bare canvas. These ‘declarations’, if we’re to see them as such, are blank: the time-honoured (if slightly laboured) shorthand for politicians’ empty promises.

The pictures themselves are distinctly easy on the eye, the soft-fade gradation and warm colours at odds with Bogacka’s allusions to societal discord. There’s no reason why art that aspires to political allegory should be visually abrasive, nor why an artist shouldn’t produce saleable work. And yet it’s a distraction that, for all their tortured symbolism, these paintings would feel right at home on the walls of someone’s Florida condominium.

Agata Bogacka: Interactionship at Edel Asanti, London, 4-26 September

article_text:
Alex Gibney, director of the new four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, said that Universal, owners of the film’s international distribution rights “wavered” over releasing the film outside North America.

Gibney was speaking to the New York Times as the film opened in the US (where it is being released by the independent distributor Bleecker Street), and appeared to confirm a story in the Hollywood Reporter that Universal, which had acquired the international rights to the film in 2023 , had got cold feet. Asked by the New York Times, “Did Universal Pictures waver in setting up its international release plans?” Gibney replied: “Yes.”

A subsequent story in Variety suggested that Universal had been concerned about “legal threats from Musk”, but that the studio had “always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally”. Gibney was asked: “So it wasn’t about legal clearances?” The film-maker replied: “You can walk and chew gum at the same time.”

However, it appears plans are back on track, as Gibney added: “We just had a meeting with [Universal], and we’re talking very concretely about a release plan.”

Gibney also said his producer Jessie Deeter, who knew Musk from two previous films, had attempted on several occasions to ask Musk to be interviewed for the film. Musk’s response was to post “Gibney is a douche” on X, the social media platform owned by Musk-founded company SpaceXAI.

In the wake of the film’s premiere at the Venice film festival, Musk posted a string of criticisms of the film and insults aimed at Gibney , including calling the film a “hit piece that misses” and threatening legal action.

Universal declined to comment further, pointing to its previous statement: “We’ve always been committed to releasing this film, and our plans haven’t changed.”

article_text:
Galerie von Vertes is staging a major survey of Pop art, debuting in London before making its way to Zurich. The new exhibition, “ Pop-ism ,” brings together work from across more than six decades—from 1946 through 2008—and by some of the movement’s most recognized names, including Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Robert Rauschenberg, Niki de Saint Phalle, Tom Wesselmann, Robert Indiana, and John Chamberlain.

London specifically is an apropos backdrop for “Pop-ism,” as Pop art first emerged in the English capital in the mid-1950s, pioneered by artists like Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi. The exhibition premieres alongside PAD London, which runs October 13–18. Following that first week, it will travel to Zurich and continue through December 4. It is a coincidental boon for Pop art fans around the globe, as the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum is also running a Pop retrospective in New York, on view through January 2027.

Claes Oldenburg, Tea Bag (1966). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

The title of the Galerie von Vertes show comes from Warhol himself, who used the term to describe the moment the long run of insular, theory-driven art movements gave way to something looser and more accessible. The show traces the shift toward approachability through a wide lens, presenting Chamberlain’s sculptures built from crushed automobile parts; Haring’s graphic, energetic cityscapes; Saint Phalle’s voluptuous Nana figures; Rauschenberg’s layered collages; and Wesselmann’s flattened, boldly colored compositions.

Complementing pieces from Pop icons are works by artists who paved the way for the then-burgeoning movement: The exhibition features Alexander Calder’s stabiles, Fernand Léger’s industrial still lifes, and Yayoi Kusama’s early soft sculptures, to name a few. Together, they illuminate a through line from Pop’s immediate predecessors to its heyday.

John Chamberlain, Potatopoultry (2008). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

What Galerie von Vertes’s exhibition makes apparent is that Pop artists share more than a visual style; they share an instinct, an openness to abandoning the serious and rarefied materials, motifs, and techniques of generations prior in favor of accessible, mass imagery, commercial processes, and materials from everyday life. Instead of approaching art as something precious and exclusive, each artist approached art-making first and foremost as a conduit for ideas, borrowing the strategies and logic of advertising, embracing repetition, and finding new aesthetic potentials from within consumer and mass culture, rather than attempting to stand outside of it. In doing so, many of the artists took on the same attributes as celebrities or brands in their own right—a phenomenon that is treated within the exhibition as an indispensable facet of the work rather than an extraneous historical fact.

Tom Wesselmann, Daytime Still Life with Blonde and Goldfish (1999). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

Galerie von Vertes also makes a case for Pop art’s long reach—both geographic and temporal—as it provided the fertile ground for successive movements, such as Neo-Pop, Minimalism, Conceptual art, and Political Pop. Accompanied by an exhibition catalog featuring a selection of important works by influential Pop artists and texts by art historian Dr. Quirine Verlinde, “Pop-ism” is a cogent exploration of what remains one of the most influential movements of the past century.

“ Pop-ism ” is on view at Galerie von Vertes through December 4, 2026.
excerpt_original: Running alongside PAD London, the exhibition brings together Warhol, Haring, Chamberlain, and more in the city where the movement first took shape in the mid-1950s.

article_text:
Berlin-based Picture Tree International has boarded international sales on “Raging Moms” (Komplizinnen), an ensemble comedy from the production company behind successes like “Weekend Rebels,” “Welcome to Germany,” “Never Look Away” and “The Lives of Others.”

PTI will screen the film as a market premiere for buyers at the upcoming American Film Market, with Leonine Studios releasing the film in German theaters on Jan. 21.

Related Stories

Hollywood Executives See Growing Market for Asian Stories, but ‘Every Movie Is Still a Fight’

'Club Kid' to Host Free Screenings for Nightlife Communities in 12 U.S. Cities (EXCLUSIVE)

Menopause, empty nests and romantic misadventures upend the lives of four women, who have had enough of being reasonable. As they abandon familiar roles and make increasingly reckless choices, their paths collide in a comedy about friendship and the messy business of starting over.

The cast is led by Laura Tonke (“Amrum,” “The People vs. Fritz Bauer”), Heike Makatsch (“The Book Thief,” “Love Actually”), Katharina Marie Schubert (“The Teachers’ Lounge”) and Anne Ratte-Polle (“Dark,” “Undine”), with Tom Schilling (“Never Look Away,” “Generation War”), Christoph Maria Herbst (“Contra,” “How About Adolf”) and Trystan Pütter (“Babylon Berlin,” “Toni Erdmann”) also starring.

“Raging Moms” is written and directed by Sonja Heiss, whose credits include “When Will It Be Again Like It Never Was Before,” which earned her a German Film Award nomination for Best Director.

A Wiedemann & Berg Film production, “Raging Moms” is produced by Johanna Bergel, Quirin Berg and Max Wiedemann, with funding from the German Federal Film Fund (DFFF), the German Federal Film Board (FFA), Medienboard Berlin-Brandenburg and FFF Bayern.

PTI’s AFM lineup also includes market screenings of a newly remastered 4K version of “The Experiment,” from “Downfall” director Oliver Hirschbiegel, and Constantin Film’s “The Perfect Holiday,” Bora Dagtekin’s sequel to “The Perfect Secret,” the German remake of “Perfect Strangers.” Selected buyers will also be offered previews of the Uruguayan period thriller “Matarifes – Hunger for Change,” directed by Rafael and Bernardo Antonaccio (“In the Quarry”), and the Swedish tech satire “Push the Button,” directed by Anton Källrot and featuring Noah Taylor.

Also upcoming on PTI’s slate include the historical biopic “Rafaela,” starring Loreto Mauleón, and “ The Stolen Child ,” the English-language, medieval fantasy epic written and directed by Sebastian McKinnon.

"今年春季，东方艺术协会（Kvost）在柏林的展览就已经亮相。如今，策展人施特凡·科尔（Stephan Koal）已成功争取到莱比锡大学作为第二站的合作伙伴。在奥古斯特广场演讲厅大楼内大学自己的画廊里，维特多夫半个多世纪前为这座城市创作的那些黑白版画迎接着来访者。除了女游泳运动员外，其余所有版画展现的都是男性：《在淋浴下》构成了与之对应的男性作品。七名年轻运动员一起站在淋浴喷头下。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这里，艺术家同样强调了集体、身体感以及运动员的日常生活。然而，这些人物也完全可以被解读为具有情色意味：高举的双臂展现着上半身，是人体艺术中的经典母夫。胸部和皮肤上溅起的水花得到了强调，生殖器也得到了详细而清晰的刻画。此外，被描绘者之间还有着含混不清的目光交流。在艺术史上，这一母题属于一个常被解读为同性恋情色意味的传统，例如丢勒的木刻版画《男澡堂》（约1496年）或托马斯·埃金斯的《游泳洞》（1884/85年）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“公开出柜是不可想象的”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在创作“青年与体育”系列的同时，维特多夫私下里作为同性恋者出了柜，并开始了与男性的初恋。展览导览手册中如是记载，该手册追溯了9位游走于地下状态与宣传之间的艺术家的生平。“维特多夫是党员，公开出柜是不可想象的，”策展人科尔解释道，“如果他是个同性恋的事情公开了，他就会被开除出党。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那些年轻、热爱运动的男性从他的国家委约创作中消失了，转而出现在他家里。“他退回到了私人领域，继续接单创作，但作品中的力量已经大不如前了，因为他剔除了个人色彩。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两德统一后，维特多夫于2004年在柏林同性恋博物馆举办了他的第一场个人展览。“我觉得难以置信的是，艺术家们是如何应对民主德国这种处境的，他们是如何找到自己的自由空间的，他们是如何在家里的沙龙中展示自己的艺术，或者又是如何彻底顺从的，”科尔说道，“这远没有得到全面梳理，最多只是部分梳理。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "民主德国在法律上比西方更自由", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "民主德国曾存在“酷儿”艺术吗？它是在什么环境下产生的？艺术和现实生活是如何变得可见的——而审查制度、国家安全部（史塔西）和文化政策又扮演了什么角色？施特凡·科尔对这些问题进行了长达三年的研究。西德活动人士的立场（如罗莎·冯·普劳恩海姆或沃尔夫冈·提尔曼斯）早已为人所知，但从东部视角探讨这一主题的文献却几乎没有。他与许多见证人以及部分已故艺术家的亲属进行了多次对话。", "links": "民主德国在法律上比西方更自由：1968年，将同性恋定为刑事犯罪的刑法第175条从民主德国的刑法典中被删除，并由“保护青年法”取而代之。尽管如此，在日常生活中同性恋仍然是一种禁忌，公开可见几乎是不可能的，史塔西也对这一群体进行了密切监视。柏林同性恋利益共同体（HIB）从1973年起试图组织起来，但因国家设置的重重障碍而告吹。在20世纪80年代，新教教会为工作小组提供了避难所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览展示了在社会主义国家的社会、意识形态和政治条件下发展起来的艺术立场。“性与艺术创作之间存在着截然不同、部分公开、部分隐蔽的联系，”施特凡·科尔在共同参观时解释道。尽管“酷儿”一词在当今意义上并未在民主德国存在，但他在这里还是刻意使用了这个词：作为一个统称，指代那些作为女同性恋、男同性恋和双性恋渴望并爱着同性的人，以及那些作为跨性别者和非二元性别者生活在传统性别观念之外的人。", 产下——当时被指定为男性性别。青少年时期，她用自己赚来的第一笔钱给自己买了一顶假发和女装。在巴勒莫，她曾因穿女裙而被拘留11周。1928年，她结识了医生兼性学家 Magnus Hirschfeld（1868–1935）。莱比锡的展柜里躺着一份所谓“变装证”的复制品，该证件允许她在街上穿女装活动。", "links": [{"text": "den Arzt und "paragraph", "text": "更改姓名的最初申请未获批准，20年代末，她开始接受性别重置手术。继多拉·里希特（Dora Richter）和沙拉克（Charlaque）之后，托妮·埃贝尔很可能是全球第三位成功实施此类医疗手术的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她通过用自己的画作支付医生费用以及在性科学研究所（Institut für Sexualwissenschaft）担任女佣来资助这些手术。在内容全面的目录中，她于1952年的一幅自画像中手拿画刷自信地注视着前方。她1956年的画作《特姆林附近的森林》（Wald bei Templin）在一个垃圾桶旁被发现，后来在Ebay上以300欧元的价格被拍卖。", "translated": true}, Wrobel）——他们所有人都以截然不同的方式回应了各自时代的条件。他们那带有传奇色彩的生平轨迹在展览中通过私人照片、报纸文章和感人的文件得到了生动的图解。例如，多罗特娅·冯·菲利普斯博恩的遗嘱就放在那里，她将自己的遗产留给了她的生活伴侣，她与对方携手走过了50多年。斯塔西（Stasi）档案生动地展现了对埃贡·弗罗贝尔的全面监视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一些作品非常直接地讲述了民主德国的酷儿生活：丽塔·“汤米”·托马斯在大量黑白照片中将自己摆拍为男性——通常带着狗。她于1931年出生于柏林，后来成为该市另类场景的核心人物。柏林墙建造后，这位宠物美容师和动物训练师将自己的公寓提供出来作为聚会场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影师安德烈亚斯·福克斯从1983年起带着相机穿梭于东柏林亚文化中，正如克里斯托夫·坦内特（Christoph Neben den Schwimmerinnen zeigen alle weiteren Blätter Männer: \"Unter der Dusche\" bildet dabei das maskuline Gegenstück. Auf den zweiten Blick sind zwei zarte Narben unter den Brustwarzen erkennbar. \"Die Position von Harry Hachmeister verweist auf die anhaltende Aktualität des Themas\", erklärt Stephan Koal. \"Gerade vor dem Hintergrund weltweiter Angriffe auf die Rechte und Lebensrealitäten queerer Menschen.\""}]

Gab es "queere" Kunst in der DDR? Und wenn ja, wie entstand sie, und wurde sie gesehen? Eine Ausstellung in Leipzig geht diesen komplexen Fragen nach und zeigt Lebenswege zwischen Untergrund und Anpassung

Die Badeanzüge sind voller Punkte, Streifen und Karos, verorten die Szene in den frühen 60er-Jahren. Der Schwarz-Weiß-Holzschnitt mit dem Titel "Jugend und Sport, Trainingsgespräch der Schwimmerinnen" zeigt 13 Frauen und Mädchen, die sich wie auf einem Fries am Beckenrand aufreihen. Die Linien sind klar, die Gesichter individuell, die Körper wirken natürlich. 1963 erhielt der Maler und Grafiker Jürgen Wittdorf von der Stadt Leipzig den Auftrag, einen Zyklus zum Thema "Jugend und Sport" für die Deutsche Hochschule für Körperkultur anzufertigen. Es entstanden fünf großformatige Holz- und Linolschnitte, die nun wieder in Leipzig hängen. "Queere Kunst in der DDR?" lautet der bewusst als Frage formulierte Titel der zugehörigen Ausstellung. Und die schaut anders auf diese Bilder, als es sich die Auftraggeber damals wahrscheinlich vorgestellt haben.

Bereits im Frühjahr war die Präsentation des Kvost, dem Kunstverein Ost, in Berlin zu sehen. Nun hat Kurator Stephan Koal die Universität Leipzig als Kooperationspartner für eine zweite Station gewinnen können. In der uni-eigenen Galerie im Hörsaalgebäude am Augustusplatz begrüßen jene schwarz-weißen Blätter die Besuchenden , die Wittdorf vor mehr als einem halben Jahrhundert für die Stadt gefertigt hat. Neben den Schwimmerinnen zeigen alle weiteren Blätter Männer: "Unter der Dusche" bildet dabei das maskuline Gegenstück. Sieben junge Sportler stehen gemeinsam unter der Brause.

Auch hier betont der Künstler Gemeinschaft, Körperlichkeit und den Alltag der Athleten. Doch die Figuren lassen sich durchaus auch erotisch lesen: Erhobene Arme, die den Oberkörper präsentieren, sind klassische Motive aus der Aktkunst. Das aufspritzende Wasser auf Brust und Haut wird betont, die Genitalien sind detailliert und deutlich ausgeführt. Dazu kommen zweideutige Blicke zwischen den Dargestellten. Kunsthistorisch steht das Motiv in einer Tradition, die oft homoerotisch gedeutet wird, etwa Dürers Holzschnitt "Das Männerbad" (um 1496) oder Thomas Eakins' "The Swimming Hole" (1884/85).

"Ein öffentliches Coming-out war undenkbar"

Parallel zur Arbeit am Zyklus "Jugend und Sport" hatte Wittdorf sein privates Coming-out als Homosexueller und erste Beziehungen zu Männern. So ist es im Begleitheft zur Ausstellung zu lesen, das die Biografien von neun Kunstschaffenden zwischen Untergrund und Propaganda nachzeichnet. "Wittdorf war in der Partei, ein öffentliches Coming-out war undenkbar", erklärt Kurator Koal. "Wenn publik geworden wäre, dass er schwul ist, wäre er aus der Partei ausgeschlossen worden."

Die jungen, sportlichen Männer verschwanden aus seinen staatlichen Aufträgen und landeten bei ihm zu Hause. "Er hat sich ins Private zurückgezogen, weiter Aufträge gemacht, aber in den Arbeiten war nicht mehr so viel Kraft, weil er das Persönliche herausgenommen hat."

Seine erste Einzelausstellung nach der Wiedervereinigung hatte Wittdorf 2004 im Schwulen Museum in Berlin. "Ich finde es unglaublich interessant, wie die Künstler:innen mit dieser Situation in der DDR umgegangen sind, wie sie ihre Freiräume gefunden haben, wie sie ihre Kunst in Salons zu Hause präsentiert oder sich komplett angepasst haben", so Koal. "Das ist noch lange nicht aufgearbeitet, höchstens teilweise."

Die DDR war juristisch liberaler als der Westen

Gab es "queere" Kunst in der DDR? Unter welchen Umständen entstand sie? Wie wurden Kunst und Lebensrealitäten sichtbar – und welche Rolle spielten Zensur, Staatssicherheit und Kulturpolitik? Über drei Jahre lang hat Stephan Koal zu diesen Fragen recherchiert. Während westdeutsche aktivistische Positionen wie die von Rosa von Praunheim oder Wolfgang Tillmans seit Langem bekannt sind, gab es zum Thema aus Ost-Perspektive kaum Literatur. Er hat viele Gespräche mit Zeitzeuginnen und Verwandten der zum Teil bereits verstorbenen Künstlerinnen und Künstler geführt.

Die DDR war juristisch liberaler als der Westen: 1968 wurde der Homosexualität kriminalisierende Paragraf 175 aus dem Strafgesetzbuch der DDR gestrichen und durch den "Jugendschutzparagrafen" ersetzt. Im Alltag galt Homosexualität dennoch als Tabu, öffentliche Sichtbarkeit war kaum möglich, und die Stasi beobachtete die Szene genau. Die Homosexuelle Interessengemeinschaft Berlin (HIB) versuchte ab 1973, sich zu organisieren, scheiterte aber an staatlichen Hürden. In den 80er-Jahren boten evangelische Kirchengemeinden Schutzräume für Arbeitskreise.

Die Ausstellung zeigt künstlerische Positionen, die sich unter den gesellschaftlichen, ideologischen und politischen Bedingungen des sozialistischen Staates entwickelten. "Sexualität und künstlerisches Schaffen stehen dabei in ganz unterschiedlichen, teils offenen, teils verdeckten Zusammenhängen", erklärt Stephan Koal beim gemeinsamen Rundgang. Auch wenn der Begriff "queer" in seiner heutigen Bedeutung in der DDR nicht existierte, hat er ihn hier bewusst verwendet: als Sammelbegriff für Menschen, die als Lesben, Schwule und Bisexuelle gleichgeschlechtlich begehrten und liebten, sowie jene, die als transgeschlechtliche und nichtbinäre Personen jenseits konventioneller Ideen von Geschlecht lebten.

Für 300 Euro bei Ebay versteigert

Ausgangspunkt sind die Lebenswege: Das ist zum Beispiel Toni Ebel, 1881 als erstes von elf Kindern geboren - dabei Zuweisung des männlichen Geschlechts. Als Jugendliche kauft sie sich vom ersten selbst verdienten Geld eine Perücke und Frauenkleider. In Palermo sitzt sie für das Tragen eines Kleides elf Wochen in Haft. 1928 lernt sie den Arzt und Sexualwissenschaftler Magnus Hirschfeld (1868–1935) kennen. In der Vitrine in Leipzig liegt eine Replik des sogenannten Transvestitenscheins, der ihr erlaubt, sich auf der Straße in Frauenkleidern zu bewegen.

Dem ersten Antrag auf Namensänderung wird nicht stattgegeben, Ende der 20er-Jahre beginnen geschlechtsangleichende Operationen. Nach Dora Richter und Charlaque ist Toni Ebel vermutlich die dritte Person weltweit, bei der eine solche medizinische Maßnahme erfolgreich durchgeführt wird.

Sie finanziert die Eingriffe, indem sie Ärzte mit eigenen Gemälden bezahlt und als Dienstmädchen am Institut für Sexualwissenschaft arbeitet. Im umfassenden Katalog blickt sie selbstbewusst mit Pinsel in der Hand von einem Selbstporträt von 1952. Ihr Gemälde "Wald bei Templin" von 1956 wurde neben einer Mülltonne gefunden und später für 300 Euro bei Ebay versteigert.

Dokumentieren, was es angeblich nicht gab

Ob Toni Ebel, Andreas Fux, Jochen Hass, Dorothea von Philipsborn, Erika Stürmer-Alex, Rita "Tommy" Thomas, Jürgen Wittdorf oder Egon Wrobel – sie alle reagierten auf die Bedingungen ihrer Zeit auf sehr unterschiedliche Weise. Ihre teils filmreifen Lebenswege werden in der Ausstellung durch private Fotos, Zeitungsartikel und berührende Dokumente illustriert. Da liegt etwa das Testament von Dorothea von Philipsborn, die ihren Nachlass ihrer Lebensgefährtin vermachte, mit der sie über 50 Jahre durch die Welt gegangen war. Stasi-Akten verdeutlichen eindrücklich die umfassende Observation von Egon Wrobel.

Einige Arbeiten erzählen sehr direkt vom queeren Leben in der DDR: Rita "Tommy" Thomas inszeniert sich auf zahlreichen Schwarz-Weiß Fotografien als Mann – oft mit Hund. 1931 in Berlin geboren, wurde sie eine zentrale Figur der alternativen Szene in der Stadt. Nach dem Mauerbau stellte die Hundefrisörin und Tiertrainerin ihre Wohnung für Zusammenkünfte bereit.

Fotograf Andreas Fux zog ab 1983 mit der Kamera durch die Ost-Berliner Subkultur und dokumentierte, wie es Christoph Tannert im Katalog schreibt, "was es angeblich nicht gab." Seine in der DDR entstandenen Fotografien würden aussehen wie "unabsichtliche Street Photography, sind in Wirklichkeit aber eine meisterhaft ins Bildliche überführte Familienaufstellung, inklusive Gay Men Posing und Demo-Vergnügen." Einmal mehr belegt diese Ausstellung, dass es keine DDR-Kunst gibt – es gibt Kunst, die in der DDR entstanden ist, geprägt von staatlichem Einfluss, Brüchen, Ambivalenzen, Macht und Anpassung.

Blonder Boy mit Einhorn und Narben

Die Verbindung ins Heute leistet Harry Hachmeister . Geboren 1979 in Leipzig, hatte er 2019 die letzte Einzelausstellung unter dem alten Namen Grit Hachmeister in der Galerie ASPN in Leipzig, im selben Jahr die erste Einzelausstellung unter dem Vornamen Harry im Projektraum für aktuelle Kunst Putte in Neu-Ulm.

"Ich mache nichts, was ich mir vorher irgendwie ausdenke, sondern jede künstlerische Idee hat ihren Ursprung in meinem Leben oder meinem Umfeld", so Hachmeister 2022 anlässlich einer Schau im Museum der bildenden Künste Leipzig. Eine kleinformatige Zeichnung zeigt einen blonden Boy mit Einhorn. Auf den zweiten Blick sind zwei zarte Narben unter den Brustwarzen erkennbar. "Die Position von Harry Hachmeister verweist auf die anhaltende Aktualität des Themas", erklärt Stephan Koal. "Gerade vor dem Hintergrund weltweiter Angriffe auf die Rechte und Lebensrealitäten queerer Menschen."

article_text:
Student competition

Providing a platform for photography students worldwide. Prizes include top Sony Digital Imaging equipment, inclusion in the London exhibition and the annual book - plus more!

Free to enter for anyone aged from 18 to 30 years-old undertaking a photography programme*

Students answer a set brief with 5 to 10 images

Up to 10 shortlisted photographers

One overall winner receives the Student Competition Winner title

Deadline for entries is 27 November 2026 at 16:00 (GMT)

2027 Student brief: Journeys

Journeys are a universal theme across cultures and languages, and can take many shapes. They have been explored in countless works of art, fiction and non-fiction, and in photography. For this year’s brief, we invite students to explore the theme of Journeys from their own perspective.

Considering the idea of Journeys in its broadest sense, we encourage you to interpret this theme in a way that feels meaningful to you. From the rites of passage that shape a child’s coming of age, to the transformations that shape our cities, to the small, day-to-day changes within a particular community, to migrations of animals across continents, life across the globe is marked by movement and change. We invite you to depict a journey of your choice, through a photographic series of five to 10 images.

Your images can be taken on any device, shot in any style, and approached from any angle you feel is best. While creative responses are encouraged, photographers must stick to the brief.

If your institution is not registered yet, you can register here . For a list of participating institutions, please see here .

*A programme refers to a formalised photography course/credit/module/foundation which is taught at higher education level, within a diploma / Bachelor of Arts / Master of Arts curriculum.

Rules

The Student competition provides a platform for photography students and universities worldwide. Students must submit series of minimum five (5) and a maximum of ten (10) images, responding to the annual brief.

1. The Competition is open to all students of photography from World Photography Organisation’s selected Universities. All Entrants must be aged between 18 and 30 years of age at the time of Competition’s deadline. All entries must confirm, on application, their acceptance of the rules of the Competition and these Terms and Conditions. Entries must be submitted by 16.00 GMT on 27 November 2026. By entering the Competition, each Entrant agrees and acknowledges that World Photography Organisation is permitted to receive his/her registration data. All personal information will be used by the World Photography Organisation in accordance with its privacy policy.

2. Students are required to submit Five (5) - Ten (10) images responding to a brief. To enter, students must ensure their institution is registered and images are submitted via www.worldphoto.org .

2.1 Images must be taken in the 18 months prior to the competition closing date of 27 November 2026. Entries should be based on the Brief outlined, information on which can be found on the Website. 2.2 Published work may have been taken in the 18 months prior to the competition closing date of 27 November 2026, but must have been first published between the dates of 1 January 2026 and 27 November 2026.

Up to 20% of work can be published at any point in time on your personal website, social media or exhibited as part of an official programme i.e. two images can be published on personal platforms at any point in time if submitting a series of 8-10 images. One image can be published at any point in time if submitting a series of 5-7 images. 2.3 Images should be no smaller than 1MB and no larger than 5MB. Images should be JPEG files. All images must be saved in the sRGB colour model and EXIF data must be left in the image file. 2.4 All Entrants, if they are selected amongst the shortlist, must be able to supply a high resolution image suitable for printing in exhibitions should the image be required. 3.1 All entries to be uploaded by 13.00 GMT on 27 November 2026.

3.2 Images from all participating students will then be judged by the selected World Photography Organisation judging panel to choose a shortlist and overall winner. The selected shortlist will be announced after being deemed suitable by the World Photography Organisation after January 1, 2027.

3.3 The overall winner will be announced in April 2027.

3.4 The decision of the World Photography Organisation is final and no negotiation will be entered into.

3.5 The World Photography Organisation reserves the right, in its sole discretion, to disqualify and remove any entry that does not comply with the following requirements, even after the entry is submitted on the Website. World Photography Organisation will not take part in dialogue with any Entrant who has been refused entry or otherwise:

3.5.1 Entries must be original and your own work

3.5.2 You have the right to make your entry available to the competition

3.5.3 Entries containing personally identifiable information about the submitter or any other person(s).

3.5.4 Entries containing any infringing, threatening, false, misleading, abusive, harassing, libellous, defamatory, vulgar, obscene, scandalous, inflammatory, pornographic or profane content.

3.5.5 Entries containing any material that could constitute or encourage conduct, which would be considered a criminal offence, give rise to civil liability, or otherwise violate any law.

3.5.6 Entries which infringe upon the copyrights, trademarks, contract rights, or any other intellectual property rights of any third person or entity, or which violate any person’s rights of privacy or publicity. This means, for example, that entries must not include:

3.5.6.1 trademarks owned by third parties;

3.5.6.2 copyrighted materials owned by third parties (including movie dialogue or musical compositions); and/or

3.5.6.3 names, likenesses, voices or other characteristics identifying celebrities or other public figures, living or dead.

3.5.7 Entries in which an Entrant has purchased or secured the rights to use stock images.

article_text:
Former Movistar Plus content boss Domingo Corral sees his production deal with HBO Max as the route to realising an ambition to make independent TV and film that is both mainstream and premium in quality.

His shock exit from the Telefonica-owned Movistar after 11 years in May 205 was followed in March with the announcement that his new career as an independent producer was taking off with a HBO production deal in place .

Announced at Series Mania this year, Sîrat exec producer Corral will work HBO Max originals exec Sarah Aubrey and Casey Bloys, both now part of senior content team at the merged Skydance business, to create scripted TV an film productions. The first project is about the disappearance of petty criminal El Nani (aka Santiago Correla) in 1980s Spain during the country’s transition out of dictatorship and into democracy.

Related Stories

'The Birds' Limited Series Starring Sarah Snook Lands At HBO For Development From Tom Spezialy, David Heyman & UGT

'Harry Potter' Series Finds Its Lily & James Potter In Jasper Talbot & Hannah Chinn; Harry Gilby To Play Charlie Weasley

“Right now, I don’t plan to make many things,” says Coral in an exclusive interview with Deadline at the MIA Market in Rome. “I have this deal, and I feel very lucky because I’ve found a place where they share the same vision that I do. It’s very important that you share the same vision with the commissioner.

Watch on Deadline

“After my exit [from Movistar], you always feel bruised. You think, ‘My God, what’s going to happen now?’ But I felt very lucky. For me, HBO is not just a client; it’s a group of people who share the same vision and very similar sensibilities.”

Guiding Corral’s outlook is his experience at Movistar, where the Spanish production community fell in love with him and his commissioning team for their approach of demanding festival-quality storytelling with the mainstream ambition of attracting big audiences. In that sense, he meshes well with the mantra at HBO.

“I ran original production at Movistar for 11 years within a telecommunications company – that’s the interesting thing,” he says. “I’m so grateful to that company for the opportunity it gave me. I had to work with engineers and finance people – people who understood numbers – and for 11 years, we made original productions at Movistar. Do you think people who look at numbers all the time would have allowed that to happen if we weren’t making quality mainstream content?

“We weren’t making niche content simply to win awards. We won many awards, but the primary objective was to retain subscribers and attract new ones, so I believe you can make quality mainstream content. I don’t see any contradiction. HBO is a very good example.”

It’s helpful that Corral spent 15 years at Turner Broadcast System, which for many years sat next to HBO in the Time Warner stable. He left there for Movistar in 2014 having risen to General Manager and SVP of Turner Iberia, overseeing operations for CNN, TCM, Boing, Cartoon Network and TNT in Spain and Portugal.

Industry support

When Corral’s exit from Movistar Plus was announced last year, there was an outpouring of anger, grief and concern from Spain’s creative community that is rarely afforded to a commissioning executive.

An open letter signed by close to 200 members of the Spanish industry , including Pedro Almodóvar and Penélope Cruz, called out the Telefonica-owned Movistar, saying Corral and his team had championed a strategy “based on respect for creators, close collaboration with independent producers and listening to all the partners they have worked with, without ever neglecting their focus on entertainment.”

Movistar was so rattled that Corral’s effective replacement on the cinema side, Guillermo Farré, would later tell Deadline , “The goal is clear, the direction of what Domingo started works on many different levels.” Speaking privately to those in the Spanish production community, the jury is still out whether his legacy of hits such as Sîrat , La Peste , La Mesías and currently smash La Bola Negra is being honored.

Movistar – which has now dropped the confusing extra ‘+’ after the ‘Plus’ in its name – won’t comment officially on the exit of Corral and his team last year, but we understand that, internally, the position is the departures were part of a wider organizational restructure that impacted several managers, and that the company feels it maintains a strong position within Spain’s audiovisual community.

Corral himself remains in the dark about his departure. “The vision I believed in was successful – not just for me, but for my team, so I don’t understand why they made that decision,” he says. “They made management changes and other things, but you would have to ask them. I don’t know why I was fired. I didn’t ask.”

Corral is speaking to Deadline in Rome directly after appearing on a panel in which he whipped a partisan crowd up by passionately advocating for commissioners and gatekeepers to make ambitious moves or risk missing the next La Bola Negra .

“I strongly believe in what I said on stage,” says Corral, a veteran Spanish industry whose urgent and open conversational style is the antithesis of the measured and media-trained lines from many other executives.

“It’s very difficult for me to behave any other way, because when you create a project, you need to have a vision,” he says. “That vision isn’t interchangeable. I can’t execute a vision I don’t believe in, and it wasn’t only me. I had an amazing team working with me. I was leading the project, but I was surrounded by incredibly talented people. Almost all of them were fired as well.”

As for Movistar Plus+ ‘s output since he left, Corral stays diplomatic. “Honestly, I’ve moved on to something new,” he says. “I’m very excited about my new life, and I don’t look backwards. What I can say is that I wish them the best, because they’re very important to the Spanish audiovisual market.”

Plans for the future

Corral’s new life outside the corporate world. In San Sebastian last year when speaking for the first time after his Movistar exit, he quipped seeing ‘independent producer’ next to his name on stage felt weird “because I still don’t know if I’m an independent producer.”

Amusingly at MIA, Corral is handed a new name for his fledgling production operation, with a giant screen at the Westin Excelsior Hotel erroneously naming him head of ‘Good Day Productions’ (a Google search shows that is the company name of another Domingo Corral, a multi-disciplinary artist based in Oakland, California.)

Corral took the misnomer in good humor, chuckling as he repeated his line about unease about his newfound independent producer status.

Corral’s overriding belief is that quality, awards-chasing, festival-style fare can – and should – also be mainstream. “There are many things without quality that fail,” he says. “Why do we have to associate the word ‘quality’ with something that isn’t commercial? People want good food, good clothes, good television shows and good films. We should all assume that quality films and series can be mainstream.”

That puts into question the assumption quality productions are usually difficult to get made. “Difficult is a different story, yes,” says Corral. “But it’s possible.”

article_text:
Capolavoro indiscusso, entrato nel repertorio di molte compagnie internazionali, Faun di Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui , è stato ora felicemente acquisito dalla MM Contemporary Dance Company e inserito nel trittico a serata della compagnia diretta da Michele Merola , che comprende La morte del cigno , una nuova creazione sempre di Cherkaoui, e Atto bianco a firma di Enrico Morelli . I tre titoli (visti al festival Torinodanza , dopo il debutto al festival Aperto di Reggio Emilia) rappresentano un altro tassello progettuale dell’ensemble di Reggio Emilia, dedicato alla rivisitazione contemporanea di titoli significativi del grande repertorio ballettistico del Novecento.

Come lo è L’après-midi d’un faune di Vaslav Nijinski nella sua iconica coreografia ispirata alla poesia di Stéphane Mallarmé e danzata sulle musiche impressioniste del Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune di Claude Debussy . Al suo debutto, nel 1912, fece scalpore per l’audace erotismo con cui il ballerino russo dava vita alla creatura mitologica nell’incontro boschivo con delle ninfe. La versione di Sidi Larbi, creata nel 2009, nell’ambito delle celebrazioni per il centenario dei Ballets Russes, al Sadler’s Wells Theatre di Londra, è un duetto inizialmente contemplato sulla musica originale di Debussy, che sfuma poi sulle note e i canti etnici del compositore Nitin Sawhney creando uno straniamento temporale.

L’incontro della creatura mitologica con la ninfa è dentro un bosco, un luogo contemplativo illuminato da una luce frastagliata, dove il fauno, metà animale e metà uomo, si risveglia da un sonno profondo. Rotola, si inarca, autocompiace. Ha movimenti muscolosi e sinuosi, qualcosa di selvaggio, di viscerale. L’arrivo di una ninfa sbucata dal buio, e l’avvicinamento carponi, risveglierà i sensi in entrambi: si attraggono dapprima timidi, aggraziati, fluidi, poi, sempre più audaci, sensuali, curiosandosi tra le gambe, intrecciando i piedi e unendo gli arti in un giocoso acrobatismo di seduzione, fino a fondersi.

Una coreografia chiara e complessa allo stesso tempo, nella sua scrittura astratta dal segno archetipico, che ha trovato nelle sfumature istintive, calde e fisiche dei bravissimi Giuseppe Villarosa e Aurora Lattanzi due interpreti perfetti.

Secondo brano della serata è la nuova creazione del coreografo belga-marocchino, il cui titolo La Morte del Cigno conserva lo stesso dell’originale del celebre assolo di Anna Pavlova creato su di lei da Fokin sulla musica del Carnevale degli animali di Camille Saint-Saëns . Cherkaoui sceglie un tappeto sonoro di ben altra fattura: una composizione elettronica – commissionata al franco-vietnamita Alexandre Dai Castaing – , dove solo in alcuni momenti riecheggiano le note di Saint-Saëns.

Per Cherkaoui il cigno agonizzante non è più solitario. La sua morte l’ha immaginata causata da uno stuolo di uccelli neri che si avventano su di lui, lo circondano, lo pressano, lo scuotono, lo trasportano in volo, lo osservano attendendo la sua fine. La danza dinamica, circolare, avvolgente dei tre corvi sembra tradire nel finale momenti di compassione verso quel cigno che mantiene la sua verticalità danzando sulle punte mentre vorrebbe sfuggire al destino. Destino al quale andrà incontro eseguendo il suo assolo con movimenti delle spalle mentre cadono dall’alto delle piume rosse e risuona il battito del cuore.

Magnifico il quartetto: Giorgia Raffetto, Nicola Stasi, Giovanni Grosso, Mario Genovese .

La coralità di tutta la compagnia arriva con Atto bianco , titolo che rimanda al balletto per eccellenza, Il Lago dei cigni, immortalato dalla musica di Pëtr Il’ič Čajkovskij, dove il “secondo atto” è emblema del regno della purezza, della grazia incorporea e del sogno romantico incarnato da Odette e dal suo stormo di fanciulle-cigno . Le simmetrie di quel mondo spirituale e armonioso non ci sono più nella bellissima coreografia di Enrico Morelli il quale, autore sensibile alla realtà del nostro tempo afflitto da tragedie e conflitti, cede il posto al bianco come «Unico colore che ci è rimasto per urlare».

Morelli pone domande e avverte: «Non ci sono cigni stasera. Ci sono corpi che cercano di non diventare cenere. Ci sono uomini che restano, mentre tutto intorno cade. Non cercate l’incanto. Cercate il fango. Cercate il Qui. Perché la tregua…la tregua è un atto di resistenza. …Guardate bene. La tregua comincia adesso».

Sono parole, insieme ad altre in più momenti dello spettacolo, dette da una voce off (dell’attore Jacopo Trebbi ) mentre intorno esplode una danza potente di corpi che, tra smembramenti e unisoni, assoli, duetti e gruppi sapientemente distribuiti nello spazio – campo di battaglia, landa umana, sala prove -, disegnano geometrie variabili, attraversamenti, collisioni; corpi bianchi, poi in body color carne, atterrati e sollevati, trascinati come dei sopravvissuti, bloccati in tableaux vivant, pulsanti di inquietudini, resistenti ai collassi.

Elemento scenico dominante è una grande bandiera bianca, avvolta, mossa, deposta, ostentata, arresa, issata, per dire, fuor di retorica, bellezza sulle brutture del mondo, resistenza, tregua, pace. Questa versione contemporanea di Morelli ispirata all’iconico titolo classico, è anche nella scelta musicale che determina la drammaturgia: ai due brani di Čajkovskij, l’ Ouverture e il Grande Adagio , stesi nello spettacolo, aggiunge le sonorità di una originale partitura elettronica di Giuseppe Villarosa (danzatore e anche compositore), scandendo così un vibrante paesaggio emotivo e visivo.

«Potete andare, ora – riprende la voce prima del buio -. Lo spettacolo è finito, ma il bianco resta. Non è il bianco della pace che avete sognato. È il bianco del vuoto, delle città spente, di chi non ha più parole. Vi abbiamo dato la tregua, ma la tregua è solo un respiro prima del prossimo colpo. … Guardateci un’ultima volta. Siamo l’ultima trincea della bellezza».
