article_text:
I feel for film critics, I really do. Tom Cruise’s latest film Digger put them in an impossible position: you can’t really talk about it without spoiling what makes it, in my eyes, a masterpiece. Or completely terrible – as many, many critics have argued over the last week, without being fully free to say why.

That is not their fault: media screenings around the world opened with a plea from Warner Bros to not spoil the film’s central reveal . This seems like it may have been a misstep, because curiosity and Cruise alone were clearly not enough to get bums on seats. Digger is now projected to lose around $150m , after taking a paltry $20m globally in its opening weekend. Warner Bros is trying to make the best of a bad situation, first crowing about the stinker reviews – “insufferable” and “smug” have been repeated a lot – then pivoting to a new sell: the Yanks don’t get it, so it must be good .

Which is a shame, because I think Digger is a remarkable film and I am going to spoil the reveal to say why – so stop reading here if you don’t want to know.

Despite the marketing, Tom Cruise isn’t really playing Digger Rockwell, a fictional, swaggering oil tycoon who is tasked with saving the world after his oil rig explodes in Greenland, causing an enormous glacier to hurtle towards Europe and guaranteed climate disaster. Cruise plays Curtis Markson, an actor who is portraying Digger onstage in a didactic, satirical play decades after the rig really exploded and left the world in ruins. The big-budget play, titled Fossil Fools, is directed and adapted by Hannah (Sophie Wilde) and funded by Rockwell’s nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), in what seems to be a tiny act of philanthropic penance to offset his family’s terrible legacy.

I have seen Digger twice already, and I think it is brilliantly audacious. Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film is the best fictional work about the climate crisis that I have seen yet, because it is also about the inability of art to speak to this moment truthfully. It is about perception and reality. And it is about our inability to distinguish the two, and how that leaves us vulnerable to the loudest, most charismatic voices in a room.

Cruise’s Curtis Markson is frustrated by Fossil Fools, complaining that he is being made to play a “cartoon” version of Rockwell so Hannah can “make some statement”. Fossil Fools is objectively terrible: the grotesque and pathetic US president (John Goodman) constantly moans about having “cancer of the asshole” for laughs, while his top brass, all gorillas, demand the chance to bomb the glacier and “blow that frozen cunt up”. One literally eats popcorn while watching Europe go underwater. And when Digger finally stands before the world to answer for his crime, he pins the blame on them; it was their demand for oil that led to disaster, all so they could have “two-day delivery of shit you don’t need”. “You want freedom to live your unsustainable lives,” he shouts. “You love oil. Let’s cut the bullshit.”

The real Digger Rockwell was a “composed, frightening, seductive psychopath”, but Curtis is being ordered to play him like a rootin’-tootin’ clown in a ten-gallon hat. “What the fuck is happening? What are we doing?” he shouts at Hannah. The two argue it out: is this meant to be a satire? Is it a farce? Is it revenge on Digger? Or is it just a bad telling of a true story, one that was never meant to go beyond the “shitty little theatre in London” where Kenny first saw it, then saved it with his big wallet and his guilty conscience?

But then Kenny steps in to deliver a speech that, in my eyes, embodies the film’s true point. “It really doesn’t matter. Satire, comedy, farce, drama – it doesn’t matter,” he tells Curtis and Hannah. “You’re both right. We’re all right. Now what?”

“Now what” is what stayed with me. I don’t think many of us need a film to tell us that climate change is a terrifying, maddening thing to live through, or that political bloviating will probably block viable solutions, or that greed is degrading us and the planet. But I do love that a blockbuster film packed with enormous stars has posed the question: what does art mean at the end of the world? And, if we are honest with ourselves, do we just want art that tells us the truth, or reinforces what we already think?

Iñárritu’s answer is the latter; we’d probably settle for a middling play with a bad title if it gave us two hours of distraction and someone to blame. We like our US presidents stupid and laughable, not stupid and terrifying. A play written at the literal end of the world, about the literal end of the world, would very likely be didactic, plodding and annoying. Did you see Don’t Look Up? We are not above Fossil Fools.

Art will never be the thing that saves us from existential threat, Digger argues – but it can give us catharsis. In the end, Curtis plays Digger as a clown and gets a euphoric standing ovation. Then an alarm goes off, signalling some horrifying reality outside – and the audience put on their gas masks and file out the theatre.

It is almost poetic that so many critics are arguing that all of Iñárritu’s metatextual postmodern faff is a lazy defence against the criticism they want to dish out: the acting/script/accent in Fossil Fools is supposed to be bad, so we can’t say Digger is bad! But I don’t think this is quite honest and it seems like every single critic has found plenty of creative ways to say Digger is bad. So many reviews seem unable to distinguish between what is Fossil Fools and what is Digger; perception and reality. Perhaps the one truth we can settle on is: you should probably go see it yourself.

Film

Digger

Tom Cruise

Alejandro González Iñárritu

title_original: Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano
editorial_title_zh: 阿彼察ポン·韦拉斯哈古执导、蒂尔达·斯文顿主演的新片《Jengira’s Magnificent Dream》由《悲情三角》墨西哥联合制片公司Piano加入制作
editorial_excerpt_zh: 曾制作鲁本·奥斯特伦德斩获金棕榈奖的《悲情三角》的墨西哥制片与发行公司Piano已加入阿彼察ポン·韦拉斯哈古的《Jengira’s Magnificent Dream》，制片人胡里奥·查韦斯蒙特斯（Julio Chavezmontes）已证实此事。蒂尔达·斯文顿将加盟该项目。……

Blurred visions distort Jengira’s sense of time and space, drawing her across various time periods. Guided by science and empathy, she becomes a living portal between past, future and spirit. Blending 1970s sci-fi aesthetics with a timeless world where cell phones are the only markers of temporal difference, the film blurs the boundaries between memory, history and the supernatural."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Popular on Variety"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Joining Swinton are Thailand’s Jenjira Pongpas (“Cemetery of Splendor”) and Sakda Kaewbuadee (“Tropical Malady”) and Canadian actor Connor Jessup (“Falling Skies”)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In an interview with Variety, Chavezmontes discussed the company’s trajectory over the past 15 years while reflecting on its approach to identifying talent and developing co-productions. He stresses that the company remains open to projects across genres and formats, prioritizing a distinctive creative vision over mainstream formula."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“If something strikes us as potentially incredible, then the format is absolutely secondary,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Piano’s international outlook has been central to its growth, says Chavezmontes, whose many credits include Lucrecia Martel’s “Our Land,” Luis Ortega’s San Sebastian Horizons-winning “The Jockey” and Abel Ferrara’s ”Siberia.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It participates in the Morelia Film Festival this year – where it’s also throwing a big anniversary party – with Chile’s submission to the Oscars, Manuela Martelli’s “The Meltdown,” which it co-produced, and with five films it distributes: Poh Si Teng’s debut docu feature “American Doctor,” “Mickey,” “The Lost Mariachis,” “Shana” and “Beauty Salon.”", "links": [{"text": "Morelia Film Festival", "url": "https://variety.com/t/morelia-film-festival/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the upcoming Ventana Sur, Piano participates in the Proyecta Co-Production Forum with “The Absence,” the debut feature of Mexico’s Jorge Sistos Moreno whose short “The Darkness” debuted at Cannes’ Critics’ Week.", "links": [{"text": "Piano participates in the Proyecta Co-Production Forum with “The Absence,”", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/markets-festivals/ventana-sur-proyecta-2026-latin-americas-rising-talent-1236911203/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The company’s approach is built on creative collaboration rather than the pursuit of awards or predictable commercial outcomes,” Chavezmontes asserts. “The secret to our success is very difficult to know,” he says. “But above all, I think it comes down to a genuine belief in cinema and a refusal to approach what we do cynically.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chavezmontes initially established Piano to make his own films, beginning with ‘Halley,” which he wrote and which Sebastían Hofmann directed. The company subsequently expanded into producing projects by other filmmakers, building relationships through international festivals, distribution and co-production partnerships."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of its most prominent collaborations emerged through “Time Share” (“Tiempo Compartido”) the film Chavezmontes wrote and produced that competed at the Sundance Film Festival in 2018. The jury, presided by Östlund, awarded it best screenplay. Following further connections with Östlund’s longtime producing partner Erik Hemmendorff and producer Philippe Bober, Piano, which had distributed Östlund’s “The Square” was approached about co-producing “Triangle of Sadness.” “Of course, the answer was an immediate yes!” he recalls.", "links": [{"text": "“Time Share” (“Tiempo Compartido”) the film Chavezmontes wrote and produced that competed at the Sundance Film Festival in 2018.", "url": "https://variety.com/2018/film/news/sebastian-hofmann-sundance-world-cinema-time-share-clip-1202669318/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film became the company’s most internationally visible production, but Chavezmontes resists defining Piano by a single title or genre. He points to projects including Mia Hansen-Løve’s “Bergman Island “and “Siberia” as examples of films whose value cannot be measured solely by their immediate reception."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We tend to be quite chameleonic in the kinds of films we make, and we like to challenge those categories,” he says. “We do that because we’re genuinely committed to exploring new things and finding stories that move us.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Chavezmontes, the key criterion when evaluating a project is whether it resonates with him as a viewer. He describes himself as an ordinary moviegoer and believes that a film capable of moving him can connect with audiences beyond the industry."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“What matters to me is whether it speaks to me and whether I feel that we can contribute to making it happen, both creatively and in terms of the other aspects of production,” he notes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Co-production as a creative engine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Reflecting on the importance of international co-productions, especially for independent cinema, he says: “Ultimately, what really defines a co-production is the people who come together to collaborate. The creative team, the technical crew – they’re the ones who actually make the films. Money simply makes it possible to hire them.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That philosophy informs Piano’s approach to projects that cross national borders. Chavezmontes argued that the exchange of ideas and creative perspectives is at least as important as the financial benefits, particularly when filmmakers seek to realize more ambitious projects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mexico’s next step: a comprehensive film policy"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chavezmontes also called for Mexico to build on its new 30% tax incentive for both homegrown and international productions by establishing a broader, long-term government policy for the audiovisual sector."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He welcomed recent initiatives, including state-level incentives in Jalisco and Morelos, but argued that Mexico needs a more comprehensive system of support comparable to those in Spain, Brazil and Colombia."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We’ve reached a point where people understand that the audiovisual sector isn’t simply a matter of cultural support,” he points out. “It’s an industrial catalyst.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He believes Mexico has the talent, infrastructure, locations and tourism sector to compete more effectively in the international production market. article_text:
Piano, the Mexican production and distribution company behind Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or-winning “Triangle of Sadness,” has boarded Apichatpong Weerasethakul ’s “Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,” producer Julio Chavezmontes has confirmed. Tilda Swinton is attached to the project.

Just like Östlund’s multi-Oscar-nominated dark comedy, “Jengira’s Magnificent Dream” dovetails with Piano’s ongoing commitment to international collaborations with filmmakers whose work challenges conventional cinematic boundaries.

Related Stories

‘Ali G: Who Iz I’ Star Morgana Robinson on Sacha Baron Cohen Not Letting Her Break Character as 'Me Julie' and Why Film Doesn’t Mock Working Class

Luke Evans on His New ITV Drama 'The Party,' Starring in 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show' on Broadway and Whether He'll Return as Bard in 'The Hunt for Gollum'

Weerasethakul’s follow-up to “Memory,” which also starred Tilda Swinton and which Piano co-produced alongside Colombia’s Burning, among others, follows Thai widow Jengira who travels to the ancient rock forest of Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka to scatter her husband’s ashes. Blurred visions distort Jengira’s sense of time and space, drawing her across various time periods. Guided by science and empathy, she becomes a living portal between past, future and spirit. Blending 1970s sci-fi aesthetics with a timeless world where cell phones are the only markers of temporal difference, the film blurs the boundaries between memory, history and the supernatural.

Popular on Variety

Joining Swinton are Thailand’s Jenjira Pongpas (“Cemetery of Splendor”) and Sakda Kaewbuadee (“Tropical Malady”) and Canadian actor Connor Jessup (“Falling Skies”).

In an interview with Variety, Chavezmontes discussed the company’s trajectory over the past 15 years while reflecting on its approach to identifying talent and developing co-productions. He stresses that the company remains open to projects across genres and formats, prioritizing a distinctive creative vision over mainstream formula.

“If something strikes us as potentially incredible, then the format is absolutely secondary,” he says.

Piano’s international outlook has been central to its growth, says Chavezmontes, whose many credits include Lucrecia Martel’s “Our Land,” Luis Ortega’s San Sebastian Horizons-winning “The Jockey” and Abel Ferrara’s ”Siberia.”

It participates in the Morelia Film Festival this year – where it’s also throwing a big anniversary party – with Chile’s submission to the Oscars, Manuela Martelli’s “The Meltdown,” which it co-produced, and with five films it distributes: Poh Si Teng’s debut docu feature “American Doctor,” “Mickey,” “The Lost Mariachis,” “Shana” and “Beauty Salon.”

In the upcoming Ventana Sur, Piano participates in the Proyecta Co-Production Forum with “The Absence,” the debut feature of Mexico’s Jorge Sistos Moreno whose short “The Darkness” debuted at Cannes’ Critics’ Week.

The company’s approach is built on creative collaboration rather than the pursuit of awards or predictable commercial outcomes,” Chavezmontes asserts. “The secret to our success is very difficult to know,” he says. “But above all, I think it comes down to a genuine belief in cinema and a refusal to approach what we do cynically.”

Chavezmontes initially established Piano to make his own films, beginning with ‘Halley,” which he wrote and which Sebastían Hofmann directed. The company subsequently expanded into producing projects by other filmmakers, building relationships through international festivals, distribution and co-production partnerships.

One of its most prominent collaborations emerged through “Time Share” (“Tiempo Compartido”) the film Chavezmontes wrote and produced that competed at the Sundance Film Festival in 2018. The jury, presided by Östlund, awarded it best screenplay. Following further connections with Östlund’s longtime producing partner Erik Hemmendorff and producer Philippe Bober, Piano, which had distributed Östlund’s “The Square” was approached about co-producing “Triangle of Sadness.” “Of course, the answer was an immediate yes!” he recalls.

The film became the company’s most internationally visible production, but Chavezmontes resists defining Piano by a single title or genre. He points to projects including Mia Hansen-Løve’s “Bergman Island “and “Siberia” as examples of films whose value cannot be measured solely by their immediate reception.

“We tend to be quite chameleonic in the kinds of films we make, and we like to challenge those categories,” he says. “We do that because we’re genuinely committed to exploring new things and finding stories that move us.”

For Chavezmontes, the key criterion when evaluating a project is whether it resonates with him as a viewer. He describes himself as an ordinary moviegoer and believes that a film capable of moving him can connect with audiences beyond the industry.

“What matters to me is whether it speaks to me and whether I feel that we can contribute to making it happen, both creatively and in terms of the other aspects of production,” he notes.

Co-production as a creative engine

Reflecting on the importance of international co-productions, especially for independent cinema, he says: “Ultimately, what really defines a co-production is the people who come together to collaborate. The creative team, the technical crew – they’re the ones who actually make the films. Money simply makes it possible to hire them.”

That philosophy informs Piano’s approach to projects that cross national borders. Chavezmontes argued that the exchange of ideas and creative perspectives is at least as important as the financial benefits, particularly when filmmakers seek to realize more ambitious projects.

Mexico’s next step: a comprehensive film policy

Chavezmontes also called for Mexico to build on its new 30% tax incentive for both homegrown and international productions by establishing a broader, long-term government policy for the audiovisual sector.

He welcomed recent initiatives, including state-level incentives in Jalisco and Morelos, but argued that Mexico needs a more comprehensive system of support comparable to those in Spain, Brazil and Colombia.

“We’ve reached a point where people understand that the audiovisual sector isn’t simply a matter of cultural support,” he points out. “It’s an industrial catalyst.”

He believes Mexico has the talent, infrastructure, locations and tourism sector to compete more effectively in the international production market. The missing element, he argued, is a stable policy framework that recognizes the economic, cultural and social value of film and audiovisual production.

An independent vision

Despite the growing scale of international production, Chavezmontes says that Piano’s guiding principle remains its belief in the projects it chooses to support.

“We make films we genuinely believe in,” he says. “And I think that conviction is what people recognize in us: that there’s an authentic vision behind Piano, rather than a cynical one.”

Source: CNC / Eric Bonté

CNC president Gaetan Bruel unveils the first ‘Lumiere Summit’

EXCLUSIVE: Warsaw is being “seriously considered” as the location of a second edition of the Lumière Summit, possibly to be held in late summer 2027, France’s CNC and the Polish Film Institute have confirmed.

A second edition in the Polish capital would continue the conversations that began at the first Lumière Summit in the south of France in September, co-chaired by French president Emmanuel Macron and South Korean president Lee Jae-myung. The event saw around 200 key figures from the film, audiovisual and video game sectors come together with political decision-makers and creative talents to discuss the challenges and opportunities for the future of cinema and the moving image.

The Polish Film Institute would drive this second edition for which no further details have yet been decided.

A follow-up conference, In The Light of the Lumière Summit, was held during last week’s Warsaw International Film Festival to discuss new opportunities for Polish-French and European co-productions. The CNC’s deputy general Olivier Henrard and the fund’s head of international affairs Jérémie Kessler were in attendance, along with France’s ambassador to Poland Étuenne de Poncins and Poland’s minister of culture and national heritage Marta Cienkowska.

“We already have a long tradition of cooperation between France and Poland with 20 co-productions in the last 10 years,” Henrard said during a discussion with Polish producer Dariusz Jablonski, the president of the Polish Film Academy.

These have recently included films such as Agnieszka Holland’s Green Border , Michal Marczak’s documentary Closure , Anne Fontaine’s Les Innocentes and Pierre Le Gall’s queer romance Flesh And Fuel .

Closer links

The conversations around the second Summit illustrate the desire to forge closer links between Polish and French filmmakers. Henrard suggested the Summit programme might provide the setting for a discussion on whether the joint German-French Minitraité co-production fund could be used as the model for a similar arrangement to be created between France and Poland.

It could also include pitching sessions of new projects by French, German and Polish producers looking for co-production partners.

Meanwhile, culture minister Cienkowska underlined how further cooperation between the French and Polish film industries is set to benefit from the staging of the ’Poland-France 2027 Season’ which will run simultaneously in both countries, promoting collaboration between cultural communities, institutions, organisations and creators.

“I want 2027 to be remembered for the beginning of new partnerships,” she said. “The best co-productions are not simply about financial agreements, but about taking creative risks and creating something that wouldn’t have existed otherwise. This is the kind of cooperation I want to encourage.”

Furthermore, an association agreement to see greater cooperation between Poland and France was signed by Arte president Heike Hempel and Polish broadcaster TVP’s director-general Tomasz Sygut at the end of the Warsaw conference. It will come into effect at the beginning of 2027.

The agreement will cover three strands: co-production with a particular interest in documentaries and support of younger and smaller production companies; the exchange of programmes such as TVP’s long- running Television Theatre ; and the expansion of its role as a media partner of film festivals.

“This agreement opens up new opportunities for co-productions and closer cooperation between filmmakers, producers and creative teams in Poland, France, Germany and beyond,” Hempel explained.

“Europe is culturally rich and diverse but we still also surprisingly know little about the lives and experiences of people in our neighbouring countries. Films and documentaries can help us to change this. They allow us to see the world with someone else’s eyes.”

Sygut described the signing as far more than a formality. “It is another step on the long road to restoring TVP’s standing and credibility.”

It is the 15th association agreement Arte has signed following similar partnerships concluded in the past with such European public broadcasters as Sweden’s SVT, Italy’s Rai Com, Finland’s YLE, Austria’s ORF and Spain’s RTVE.

BFI’s Mia Bays corrects the record as she leaves Filmmaking Fund: “People thought I ran the LFF, the archive, and BFI Southbank”

article_text:
Film

Hell Takes the Form of State Repression in 1971’s “The Devils”

Ken Russell’s film designed by Derek Jarman, newly released in a 4K restoration, mirrors the horrors unfolding outside our windows.

The Devils (photo Screen Archives via Getty Images)

Before Derek Jarman became known for his anachronistic, queer film adaptations of the lives of Saint Sebastian, Caravaggio, Edward II, and even the Passion of Jesus, the English artist and activist worked as a set designer. This facet of Jarman, who died from AIDS-related illnesses in 1994, has recently come to the fore with the hyped release of the 4K restoration of Ken Russell's scandalous 1971 horror film The Devils , screening at the IFC Center, Brooklyn Academy of Music, and Nitehawk cinemas in New York in the coming weeks.

Adapted from Aldous Huxley's 1952 book The Devils of Loudun and John Whiting's 1961 play The Devils , the film is set in the castled town of Loudun, France, in 1634, in the aftermath of the Huguenot Rebellions against the French state's attempts to consolidate the power of the Crown and the Catholic Church. It opens with an image of a near-naked, genderqueer King Louis XIII performing on a half-shell on a theater stage à la Botticelli's “Venus” before shifting to Loudun, the site of a famous scandal wherein Ursuline nuns reportedly experienced bouts of demonic possession. The blame for this hysteria is strategically placed on a secular priest by the name of Urbain Grandier (played by a mustached Oliver Reed), who was subsequently tried and executed for his alleged crimes.

Grandier's entrapment by his enemies comes to comment on a larger evil that comes not from one poorly behaved individual but from the totalitarian powers that knock down the town's walls immediately following his burning at the stake.

"At the time that I made The Devils, I was a devout Catholic, and secure in my faith," Russell recalled in an interview in Sight and Sound in 1995, addressing the controversies surrounding the film's highly sexual depictions of nuns, priests, and even a fallen crucifix that becomes a sex object in a frenzied exorcism-cum-orgy.

“For myself, although I am not a political creature, I always viewed The Devils as my one political film. To me, it was about brainwashing, about the state taking over,” he added.

The Devils , shot on July 22, 1971 (photo Staff/Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

News

Massive King Ramses II Statues Unearthed in Egypt

The two sculptures were discovered after a citizen found a hieroglyph-etched stone on his property.

The Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the discovery of the remains of two enormous statues depicting King Ramses II in the village of Behbeit Al-Hagar, a known archaeological site in the Nile Delta. The artifacts were uncovered after a citizen notified antiquities authorities about finding a stone with hieroglyphic inscriptions on his property.

Behbeit Al-Hagar is best known for the ruins of the Iseion, an ancient Egyptian temple devoted to the goddess Isis.

Per the Ministry's press statement, the excavation yielded one carved stone head of Ramses II wearing the double crown that signified the pharaoh's unified rule over Upper and Lower Egypt. The head is around 5'3" (1.6m) tall, indicating that the height of the entire statue would likely have exceeded 27 feet (8.5m) — a scale connoting immense artistic significance. Remains of the upper portion of the statue's back pillar were also found nearby, bearing an inscription of the King's Horus name: “Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat.”

"paragraph", "text": "1876年出生于爱媛县松山市的非水曾在东京美术学校（现东京艺术大学）学习日本画，但在求学期间与洋画家黑田清輝交流的契机下，踏上了图案设计之路。毕业后，他在大阪的三和印刷店图案部展露才华，于1905年再次进京。在中央新闻社工作的同时，作为三越的嘱托设计师开始活动，不久便被破格提拔为图案主任。此后，他涉足海报、书籍装帧、包装设计等丰富多彩的工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展第1章以摘要形式介绍非水的代表作。此外，序章通过家族照片与影像资料，聚焦非水与川越的纽带。会场播放的由非水拍摄的影像，既是能一窥川越祭盛况的现存最古老珍贵影像资料，同时也能让人感受到庆典的热闹与节日般的氛围。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "走近《非水百花谱》的全貌", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在继续三越工作的同时不断积累图案家职业生涯的非水。然而在1918年1月，为了将更多时间用于自身的研学与创作，他做出了将三越的工作减至每周2天的决定。其成果之一，便是本展的主题《非水百花谱》。该作由大正时代的春阳堂出版，是一部历时2年、大约每月完成5幅图、共计集结100幅图的版画集。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2-25.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "《非水百花谱》书函 大正11年（1922） 公益财团法人平野美术馆 《非水百花谱》完结后，赠予集齐100幅图的购买者的书函箱", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "流传于川越市内的非水疏散资料中包含该作原作71幅，该馆于2023年首次将其公开。此后经过持续调查，又发现了新的原作，已确认的原作总计达112幅。针对共100幅图的版画集却有112幅原作这一事实，其中未刻版原作有38幅也浮出水面。会场中除这些原作外，还将通过展板介绍目前藏处不明的原作，整体构成旨在追溯非水为此作创作的原作全貌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，展示的顺序也颇具特色。《非水百花谱》并未按照季节等规律制作，因此通常多按发行顺序展出，但本展则是按原作的写生年月日排列。这使得观众能够更具体地追寻非水在创作过程中层层叠加的巧思等。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/3-25.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "会场风景：原作配大 A字框，版画配稍小框进行展示，让人能轻松辨别哪一件是原作", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "压轴的百花缭乱 用原作与版画领略《非水百花谱》的魅力", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一面墙壁上错落有致地排列着花谱，宛如百花缭乱。您可以从稍远处整体远观，也可以靠近端详细节，从各种角度享受观赏的乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "首先登场的是“口红水仙”原作。被认为创作于最初期的这幅作品遗憾的是并未制成版画，但画面中设一矩形、并将几乎原大尺寸的花朵收纳其中的构图，在全部100幅图中一以贯之。在绘制这幅原作前，整体构图的方针想必就已经确定了。另一方面，背景虽施以淡粉色，但在发行的版画中却利用了纸张本身的底色，由此可见在创作过程中表现手法曾有过变更。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4-25.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "〔口红水仙〕 大正7年（1918）4月 爱媛县美术馆", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最早被制成版画的原作是“木瓜”。杂志《新家庭》的封面也能看到非常相似的构图，但由于它也是《新家庭》第1辑收录的图，对非水来说或许是一朵饱含感情的花。原作以铅笔勾勒轮廓线，并用水彩柔和着色，而版画中的色调则显得稍稍清晰一些。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/5-24.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "从右起：“木瓜” 大正7年（1918）4月 非水疏散资料、《非水百花谱》第1辑“木瓜” 大正9年（1920）3月20日 公益财团法人平野美术馆、《新家庭》第5卷第3号 封面“木瓜” 大正9年（1920）3月 非水疏散资料", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "非水虽然主张“尽量描绘自然的状态”，但仍将花朵巧妙地收纳于既定的矩形之内。其中部分作品能让人微微感受到艺术加工的痕迹，这或许正体现了他旨在追求不同于博物画宗旨的图谱。从中可以感受到对自然的观察眼光与身为画面设计图案家的审美感达到了平衡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在创作途中，也进行了各种尝试。这里展出的是将两幅原作组合成一件作品的成果。原作展现出极高的完成度，但可知在实际制作版画的阶段，又加入了进一步的巧思。经过这些反复试错与细微调整，《非水百花谱》得以诞生。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/6.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "从左起：“夏枯草 钓舟草” 大正7年（1918）7月21日 爱媛县美术馆、《非水百花谱》第13辑“钓舟草” 大正10年（1921）8月28日 公益财团法人平野美术馆、“钓舟草” 大正9年（1920）10月10日 非水疏散资料 观察发行的版画可知，通过裁切左侧原作中的夏枯草、并加入右侧原作，最终整合成了以钓舟草为主体的作品", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "竟然做到这一步！？超豪华企划版画惊人的内容", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《非水百花谱》购买者手中收到的，不仅仅是精致美丽的版画。其中还附带了植物解说、照片、解说附图、拓印实物叶片的印叶画，甚至还有采用与版画不同构图来描绘植物的剪影画（“灯影式写生图”，以下简称“灯影图”）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "惊人的是，除了解说文之外，这些全部出自非水之手（照片也大部分由非水拍摄）。将灯影图、写生图等加入100幅版画中，其数量达数百点之多。以每月5点的节奏进行写生并制作原画，本身就是一项大工程。再加上还要经手丰富多彩的资料，从中不难看出非水对这一策划是何等热心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/7-19.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "从右起：《非水百花谱》第10辑“旱金莲”、同解说 均为川越市立美术馆藏", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/8-17.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "从右起：灯影式写生图印刷在解说的背面。版画背面贴有明确标明植物名、雕刻师、印刷师的标签", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "明治时期以后，从木版向其他媒介过渡的趋势不断蔓延，到了大正时期这种潮流更加强劲。在这样的时代里，出版商推出了费工费时的豪华企划，而非水则继续执笔，力求将其打造为不仅限于美丽的版画集。可以说，《非水百花谱》正是一部兼具艺术性与丰富资料价值的倾心之作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该作于1922年完成全部100幅图，获得了高度评价。然而就在次年，关东大地震将所有版木全部化为灰烬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "大正版与昭和版，复刻所带来的改变", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因地震失去了版木的《非水百花谱》，其原作本身却安然无恙。于是春阳堂于1929年根据幸免于难的原作制作了新的版木，推出了复刻版。昭和版中有4幅作品被替换为了其他作品，此外还将大正版中上下印倒的作品纠正为正确方向等，进行了细致的修正。会场中也展出了对应替换的3幅原作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "附属资料也发生了变化。大正版中印在解说背面的灯影图，在昭和版中作为独立的版画被收录。由此，每1幅图原本由“版画”和“解说/灯影图”构成的2件套，变成了加上作为版画印刷的灯影图的3件套，显得愈发豪华。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会场中还展出了珍贵的灯影图版下绘。通常情况下，版下绘会贴在版木上一同雕刻掉，因此作为版画完成的作品的版下绘是不会留存下来的。也就是说，这幅版下绘是未曾刻版的作品。这样看来，灯影图中或许还存在其他未被版画采用的图稿。光是想象非水究竟画了多少种植物的工作量──就令人顿觉思绪飘渺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/9-13.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "《非水百花谱》灯影式写生图原作“八角金盘” 大正8年（1919）4月11日 个人藏", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，还介绍了非水自己将植物写生图整理成册的资料。这份清单成为了本次原作调查中的比对线索，使得囊括非水为百花谱所绘原作成为可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/10-13.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "〔《非水百花谱》候选植物一览〕 昭和5年（1930） 个人藏", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过对比原作、版画以及附属资料，本展不仅能让观众领略植物之美，还能触及非水对构图与表现形式不断追求的创意巧思。此外，作为首个全面汇集《非水百花谱》原作的展览，其扎实的厚重感也极具品味。本展负责人、策展人折井贵惠表示：“像这样对比观赏原作与版花的展览，今后可能不会再有了。为了让大家觉得这就是决定版，我们进行了全面收罗。”不妨在漫步被称为小江户的川越之余，前去探访非水倾尽心血的百花谱吧。（撰文·虹）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "【前瞻】“诞辰150周年 杉浦非水与《非水百花谱》”川越市立美术馆10月17日起开幕 走近作家倾注心血的木版植物图谱全貌的意欲之作特别展", "translated": true}]

article_text:
日本のグラフィックデザインの先駆者・ 杉浦非水 （1876～1965年）。その代表作『非水百花譜』を特集する展覧会「生誕150年 杉浦非水と『非水百花譜』」が、川越市立美術館（埼玉県）で開催中です。会期は12月13日まで。

川越市には非水の妻・ 翠子 の実家があり、非水は戦時中、作品や資料をそこへ避難させていました。同館では2023年、これらを「非水疎開資料」として初公開。なかでも、新たに発見された版画集『非水百花譜』の原画は、卓越した描写力と美しさで注目を集めました。

本展では、原画と大正時代に刊行された版画集を比較しながら、未版刻（版画化されていない原画）や、付属資料「灯影式写生図」、復刻された昭和版『非水百花譜』にも着目。作品の構想から刊行までの工夫と、この企画に投じた非水の情熱を紹介します。

生誕150年 杉浦非水と『非水百花譜』

会場：川越市立美術館 企画展示室（埼玉県川越市郭町2丁目30番地1）

会期：2026年10月17日（土）～12月13日（日）

開館時間：9:00～17:00 ※入場は16:30まで

休館日：月曜日（ただし11月23日は開館）、11月24日（火）

観覧料：一般700円、大学生・高校生350円、中学生以下無料

詳しくは 公式サイト へ

図案家・杉浦非水

今まさにこちらへやって来ようとしている黄色い電車と、それを待つ華やかな装いの人々。杉浦非水の名を知らなくても、このポスターには見覚えがあるのではないでしょうか。

1876年、愛媛県松山市に生まれた非水は、東京美術学校（現・東京藝術大学）で日本画を学びますが、在学中に洋画家・黒田清輝と交流を持ったことを契機に、図案家の道へと進みます。卒業後は大阪の三和印刷店の図案部で才能を伸ばし、1905年に再び上京。中央新聞社で働くかたわら、三越の嘱託デザイナーとして活動を始め、やがて図案主任に抜擢されます。その後はポスターや装幀、パッケージデザインなど、多彩な仕事を手がけました。

本展の第1章では、非水の代表作をダイジェストで紹介。また、序章では、家族写真や映像資料を通して、非水と川越のつながりに目を向けます。会場で流れる非水が撮影した映像は、川越祭りの様子がわかる現存最古の貴重な映像資料であると同時に、祭りの賑わいや、ハレの日らしい空気も感じられます。

『非水百花譜』の全貌に迫る

三越の仕事を続けながら図案家としてキャリアを積んでいった非水。しかし1918年1月、自身の研究と制作に多くの時間を充てるため、三越の仕事を週2回に減らすという決断をします。その成果の一つが、本展の主題である『非水百花譜』でした。大正時代に春陽堂から刊行された同作は、約1か月に5図ずつ、2年をかけて全100図を揃えた版画集です。

川越市内に伝わる非水疎開資料には、同作の原画が71図含まれており、同館は2023年にこれらを初公開しました。その後も調査を続けた結果、新たな原画が発見され、確認された原画は計112図にのぼります。全100図の版画集に対して原画が112図あること、そしてそのうち未版刻の原画が38図あるということも明らかになりました。会場ではこれらに加え、現在所蔵先が確認できていない原画もパネルで紹介されるなど、非水が本作で制作した原画の全貌を追うことができる構成になっています。

また、展示の順序にも特徴があります。『非水百花譜』は、季節順などの規則に沿って制作されていなかったため、通常は発行順に展示されることが多いのですが、本展では原画の写生年月日順に並べています。これにより非水が制作の過程で重ねた工夫などを、より具体的にたどることができます。

圧倒の百花繚乱 原画と版画で見る『非水百花譜』の魅力

壁一面に花譜がずらりと並ぶ様子は、まさしく百花繚乱。少し離れて全体を眺め、近づいて細部を確かめるなど、さまざまな角度から鑑賞を楽しむことができるでしょう。

最初に登場するのが「口紅水仙」の原画です。最初期に描かれたと考えられるこの作品は、残念ながら版画にはなっていませんが、画面に矩形を設け、その中にほぼ原寸大の花を収める構図は、百図を通して一貫しています。この原画を描く前に、全体の構図の方針が決められていたのでしょう。一方で、背景は淡いピンクで彩られていますが、頒布された版画では紙地の色を生かしており、制作過程で表現が変更されたことがうかがえます。

最も早く版画化された原画は「 木瓜 」です。雑誌『新家庭』の表紙にもよく似た構図が見られますが、百花譜第1輯所収の図でもあることから、非水にとって思い入れのある花だったのかもしれません。原画は鉛筆で輪郭線を描き、水彩で柔らかく彩色していますが、版画では色味がややはっきりしているのがわかります。

非水は「なるべく自然の状態を描く」としながらも、決められた矩形の中に花を巧みに収めています。中にはわずかに脚色を感じるものもありますが、博物画とは趣旨の異なる図譜を目指していたことの表れなのかもしれません。そこには自然を観察する目と、画面をデザインする図案家としてのセンスが両立しているように感じられます。

制作の途中では、さまざまな試みも行われました。こちらは二つの原画を組み合わせ、一つの作品に仕立てたもの。原画は高い完成度を誇りますが、実際に版画を制作する段階で、さらなる工夫が加えられていたことがわかります。こうした試行錯誤や細かな調整を経て、『非水百花譜』は作られていきました。

ここまでやる⁉ 超豪華企画版画の驚くべき内容

『非水百花譜』の購入者の手元に届いたのは、精緻で美麗な版画だけではありません。植物の解説や写真、解説附図、実物の葉を摺った印葉に加え、版画とは異なる構図で植物を描いたシルエット画（「灯影式写生図」、以下「灯影図」）まで付属していました。

驚くべきことに、解説文を除くこれらは、すべて非水が手がけたもの（写真も大部分が非水撮影）。100図の版画に灯影図や写生図などを加えると、その数は数百点にのぼります。ひと月5点のペースで写生し、原画を制作するだけでも大仕事。そのうえ多彩な資料まで手がけたことからも、非水がいかにこの企画に熱心だったかがうかがえます。

明治期以降、木版からほかのメディアへと移行する動きが広がり、大正期にはその流れがさらに強まっていきました。そうした時代に、版元は手間のかかる豪華な企画を打ち出し、非水は美しいだけにとどまらない版画集となるよう、筆を動かし続けました。『非水百花譜』は、まさに芸術性と資料としての充実ぶりを兼ね備えた、渾身の版画集と言えるでしょう。

同作は1922年に全100図が完結し、高い評価を得ました。しかしその翌年、関東大震災によって版木がすべて焼失してしまったのです。

大正版と昭和版、復刻によって変わったもの

震災で版木が失われた『非水百花譜』ですが、原画そのものは無事でした。そこで春陽堂は1929年、被害を免れた原画をもとに新たな版木を起こし、復刻版を制作します。昭和版では4図が別の作品に差し替えられたほか、大正版で天地逆に摺られていた作品が正しい向きに改められるなど、細かな修正も加えられました。会場では、差し替えに該当する原画も3図展示されています。

付属資料にも変更がありました。大正版では解説の裏面に印刷されていた灯影図が、昭和版では独立した版画として収められたのです。これにより、1図につき「版画」と「解説／灯影図」の2枚セットだった構成が、版画として摺られた灯影図を加えた3枚セットとなり、いっそう豪華になりました。

会場では、灯影図の貴重な版下絵も展示されています。通常、版下絵は版木の上に乗せて木とともに彫ってしまうため、版画として完成した作品の版下絵が残ることはありません。つまりこの版下絵は、未版刻のもの。そうなると、灯影図にも、版画に採用されなかった図がほかにも存在する可能性が考えられます。非水がいったい何点の植物を描いたのか──その仕事量を想像するだけで気が遠くなりそうです。

また、非水自身が植物写生図をリストにまとめた資料も紹介されています。このリストが、今回の原画調査において照合の手がかりとなり、非水が百花譜のために描いた原画を網羅することが実現しました。

原画と版画、そして付属資料を見比べることで、植物の美しさだけでなく、構図や表現を追求し続けた非水の創意工夫にも触れられる本展。さらに『非水百花譜』の原画を包括した初の展覧会という、骨太な面も味わえます。本展担当学芸員の折井貴恵さんは、「ここまで原画と版画を比較して見る展覧会は、これで最後になるかもしれない。決定版と思っていただけるよう、網羅しています」と語ります。小江戸と称される川越の散策とあわせて、非水渾身の百花譜に会いに行ってみてはいかがでしょうか。 （ライター・虹）

article_text:
A new player is in town. Upstart Mexican distributor Caos Cine , founded by Regina Serratos and Eduardo Diaz Casanova, has launched at the Morelia Film Festival (FICM) with its first pickup, “The Huntress.” The debut feature of Susanne Andrews Correa marks its Mexican premiere Oct. 19 at the fest, where it competes.

“Caos is here to shake up the industry, opening up new opportunities for films to find a distribution path tailored to their needs and receive the individual attention they deserve,” said Diaz Casanova who also runs production company Peninsula Films & Entertainment, which he founded with his brother, Gabriel Diaz Casanova.

Dalton Smith vs. Alberto Puello Livestream: Here’s Where to Watch the WBC Junior Welterweight Title Boxing Match Online

The first pic in Caos’ Mexican distribution slate, “The Huntress” is toplined by “Emilia Pérez” star Adriana Paz, a Cannes 2024 Best Actress winner along with the rest of the female ensemble cast in the musical drama.

Popular on Variety

“We are deeply moved by the opportunity to share this emotionally resonant story with audiences. Supporting the creative team and championing emerging talent are central to our mission. We are incredibly proud to welcome the only Latin American film selected for Sundance 2026 to our catalog and to bring it to Mexican audiences for the first time at FICM,” added Serratos, who previously led distribution at Pimienta Films and coordinated distribution at Piano from 2015 to 2020.

Based on real-life events, Paz plays Luz who sets out to kill a serial rapist on the loose in a bid to keep her 14-year old daughter and other young factory workers safe. As events unfold in the border town of Ciudad Juárez, she is forced to confront the consequences of her actions.

Beginning in 2018, Andrews Correa made repeated trips to Ciudad Juárez. There she spoke with factory workers, journalists, filmmakers, activists, psychologists, social workers, public officials and mothers of disappeared women to ground “The Huntress” in the lived realities of the city and approach a complex issue with nuance and sensitivity.

“’The Huntress’ is both a love letter to this resistance and a warning about the injustices that fuel it,” she said.

Filmed in Ciudad Juárez and Mexico City, “The Huntress” was produced by Zafiro Cinema , founded in 2018 by Gabriela Maire (“The Good Girls”) and Edher Campos (“Huesera: The Bone Woman”), alongside U.S.-based The Population , led by Mynette Louie (“Swallow”).

The 24th Morelia Film Festival opened on Oct. 16 and wraps on Oct. 25.

article_text:
Del regreso de Carrie a una historia criminal ambientada en Los Ángeles, estas son las cinco series que recomendamos para disfrutar este fin de semana en las principales plataformas de streaming.

Si estás buscando algo nuevo para ver este fin de semana, las plataformas de streaming renuevan sus catálogos con propuestas para todos los gustos. Desde el terror y el suspenso hasta la comedia dramática, hay cinco series que merecen un lugar en tu lista. En Cinéfilos, repasamos qué ver en Netflix , Prime Video , Apple TV+ , Disney+ y HBO Max .

Carrie – Prime Video

La nueva adaptación de Carrie , basada en la novela de Stephen King, llega con una propuesta que traslada la historia de terror a los tiempos actuales. Desarrollada por Mike Flanagan, esta versión presenta a una joven que debe enfrentarse al despiadado ecosistema de su instituto tras la repentina muerte de su padre.

Interpretada por Summer H. Howell, Carrie atraviesa una etapa marcada por la presión constante, la crueldad de sus compañeros y el impacto de las redes sociales. A medida que despiertan sus misteriosos poderes telequinéticos, la adolescente deberá lidiar con una situación que amenaza con cambiarlo todo.

Con Mike Flanagan al frente, la producción propone una nueva mirada sobre uno de los relatos más conocidos de Stephen King, con el terror adolescente como eje central.

Bajo la superficie – Netflix

Para quienes buscan una historia de misterio con elementos de terror, Bajo la superficie ( Below ) es una alternativa para tener en cuenta. La miniserie canadiense cuenta con seis episodios y presenta una amenaza inesperada en un pequeño pueblo de Terranova.

Estrenos de Prime Video en noviembre de 2026: todas las series y películas que llegan a la plataforma

Gordon llega a Netflix: la nueva serie de Pablo Trapero con Rodrigo de la Serna presentó su tráiler

La tranquilidad de sus habitantes se ve alterada cuando una misteriosa criatura marina comienza a sembrar el terror. En medio de la incertidumbre, un curtido pescador y su familia se convierten en la única esperanza de sus vecinos.

Con Josh Hartnett, Mackenzie Davis y Charlie Heaton entre sus protagonistas, la producción combina suspenso, intriga y monstruos en una historia que pone a prueba a toda una comunidad.

Pequeños profetas – Apple TV+

Si preferís una propuesta que combine comedia y drama con un toque fantástico, Pequeños profetas ( Small Prophets ) puede ser una buena elección. La serie sigue a Michael Sleep, un hombre excéntrico que lleva una vida aparentemente ordinaria mientras continúa aferrado a la esperanza de reencontrarse con Clea, su pareja desaparecida hace siete años.

Su rutina cambia cuando decide experimentar con una antigua receta que combina agua de lluvia, estiércol de caballo y bastante alquimia. El objetivo es crear homúnculos, pequeños seres mágicos capaces de predecir el futuro.

Con la esperanza de encontrar una respuesta sobre el paradero de Clea, Michael se embarca en una búsqueda tan insólita como personal. Creada y protagonizada por Mackenzie Crook, la ficción británica mezcla humor, fantasía y una historia atravesada por la pérdida y la incertidumbre. Además, ya fue renovada para una segunda temporada.

The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall – Disney+

El universo criminal de Snowfall se expande con The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall , una serie ambientada en Los Ángeles durante la década de 1990, cuando el crack transformaba las calles y redefinía el poder en distintos barrios de la ciudad.

La historia pone el foco en los territorios controlados por los Bloods y los Crips, que se convierten en el epicentro de una escena musical emergente en South Central. En ese contexto, el crimen organizado, las disputas territoriales y la cultura urbana se entrecruzan en un relato que explora una etapa decisiva para la ciudad.

Con una propuesta que combina drama y crimen, la ficción busca ampliar el universo de Snowfall y ofrecer una nueva perspectiva sobre el entorno social y cultural que marcó aquella época.

Youth – HBO Max

Para cerrar las recomendaciones, Youth propone una comedia dramática británica centrada en las complicaciones de la vida adulta y los vínculos familiares. La serie sigue a una mujer divorciada de 50 años que intenta encontrar un equilibrio entre su vida amorosa, el cuidado de sus padres y las responsabilidades que implica acompañar a su hijo adulto.

Con Sharon Horgan y Rupert Friend entre sus protagonistas, la ficción aborda las dificultades de reorganizar la propia vida cuando las obligaciones familiares y los deseos personales parecen avanzar en direcciones opuestas.

A través de situaciones cotidianas, la producción explora las relaciones, las segundas oportunidades y los desafíos de una etapa en la que volver a empezar puede resultar tan complicado como necesario

article_text:
Keanu Reeves is set to star in the Netflix action movie “ Maelstrom ” after “Reacher” actor Alan Ritchson dropped out of the project.

“Carry-On” filmmaker Jaume Collet-Serra is directing “Maelstrom.” It revolves around a Federal Marshal who is guarding the fiancée of an arms dealer who is seeking witness protection as she prepares to testify against him. Events unfold over one evening as a hurricane rolls in, blocking communication from the outside world and preventing reinforcements from arriving. Together, the duo has to fight the onslaught of men working for the arms deal while dealing with the natural disaster outside their window.

Related Stories

Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal

Page Six Hollywood first reported on Reeves’ casting, though it’s unclear why Ritchson is departing the movie.

Popular on Variety

Screenwriter Mark Bianculli (“How to Rob a Bank”) is polishing the script from a first draft by late writer Gregory Fitzpatrick.

Netflix is reviving the film, which was originally sold as a spec script to Warner Bros. in 1993 by producer Jeff Robinov when he was an agent. At the time, Variety reported that “Maelstrom” was “widely described as ‘Diehard’ in a hurricane” and went for roughly $225,000 to $ 625,000. (Now that’s closer to $500,000 to $1.4 million, adjusted for inflation over 33 years.) This is the first project under Robinov’s new Netflix deal. The former Warner Bros. Pictures president has shepherded billion-dollar franchises like “The Dark Knight” trilogy and “The Hangover.”

Reeves has cemented his status as an action star through franchises like “The Matrix” and “John Wick.” Last year, he made his Broadway debut in “Waiting for Gadot” alongside his “Bill & Ted” co-star Alex Winter. He’s currently in talks to lead James Wan’s next movie “The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil” for Paramount, and he will reprise his voice role as Shadow in 2027’s “Sonic the Hedgehog 4.”

article_text:
Each week we highlight the noteworthy titles that have recently hit streaming platforms in the United States. Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups here .

Buddy (Casper Kelly)

A mix of Barney and Blue’s Clues , the TV program Buddy follows a large pink unicorn who, alongside a supporting cast of anthropomorphized house objects, teaches the program’s children a new lesson each episode. All of the show’s elements—the colorful sets, the ’90s outfits the children wear, the songs they sing—point to Kelly’s deep understanding of the aesthetics and rules of the world that he subverts. – Caleb H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

The Death of Robin Hood (Michael Sarnoski)

How many times has the story of Robin Hood been told? How many books have been written, how many movies made about the outlaw? With The Death of Robin Hood , writer-director Michael Sarnoski goes back to the source. Rather, the supposed sources. The earliest stories of Robin Hood were ballads told by commoners across England. These tales tell of an outlaw who does not give anything stolen to the poor, instead taking pleasure in killing the rich. In the medieval ballad “Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne,” Robin beheads Gisborne and sticks his head on a spike. – Dan M. ( full review )

Where to Stream: HBO Max

Hanging by a Wire (Mohammed Ali Naqvi)

A brisk docu-thriller that could do more with the richness of the players it chronicles, Mohammed Ali Naqvi’s Hanging by a Wire is not without thrills and human drama. Yet it seems focused more on a death-defying rescue than on what could be done to prevent this from happening again. – John F. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Hope (Na Hong-jin)

It’s never night in Hope Harbor. At least so long as we’re there. The eschatological events of writer-director Na Hong-Jin’s high-octane, highly anticipated Hope unfold over the course of one long, grueling, nonstop chase of a day for its rag-tag team of small-town South Korean cops, yokels, and hicks, an ensemble that ranges from heroic to hilarious in this blathering creature-feature phantasm. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

In the Mouth (Cory Santilli)

One of the most impressive American indies I’ve seen in the last year sets Free Time and Dad & Step-Dad star Colin Burgess in a surreal comedy. Cory Santilli’s In the Mouth premiered at the Slamdance Film Festival and has now arrived digitally.

Where to Stream: Fandor

Rose of Nevada (Mark Jenkin)

The films of Mark Jenkin ooze a hypnotic, seasick sensibility; to watch them is to be lulled by their restless jumps through time and space, their ability to convert his home turf of Cornwall into a suspended world where facts and visions collide in stupefying dioramas. The director is a spinner of wandering tales, never fueled by linear plots so much as ambient forces: a ticking clock, gusts of wind, the distant roaring of waves. His dramas tend to pull your gaze from people and toward the inanimate objects that litter their surroundings. It’s here––in the interstice between the fictional foreground and non-fictional background––that the actual story often lies. – Leonardo G. ( full review )

Where to Stream: MUBI

Sacrifice (Romain Gavras)

It’s not too grand a statement to say the environment you watch a film in will heavily impact how you feel about it. This was the case with Sacrifice , a supposed satire of the uber-rich and celebrity worship that, viewed in the context of a film festival’s gala world premiere where every big name in the credits was accompanied by hooting from the audience, couldn’t help ringing a little false. – Ethan V. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Netflix

The Sun Never Sets (Joe Swanberg)

It’s been nearly a decade since Joe Swanberg last sat in the director’s chair. What does the preeminent king of mumblecore have up his sleeve now? More of the same, essentially. For those familiar with work such as Drinking Buddies , Digging for Fire , and Happy Christmas , the filmmaker’s The Sun Never Sets won’t pack many surprises; his low-budget, loose rhythm in assembling a set of characters and placing them under a quasi-rom-com premise to bicker and banter remains firmly intact. – Mitchell B. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

title_original: Tatiana Trouvé’s Art Is All About Getting Lost and Found and Lost Again
editorial_title_zh: Tatiana Trouvé 的艺术全关于迷失、重逢与再次迷失
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位艺术家在 Xavier Hufkens 画廊举办了她的首场个展，展期至 10月31日。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我把时间都花在绘制地图上，”塔蒂亚娜·特鲁韦（Tatiana Trouvé）在我和她漫步于她位于布鲁塞尔的 Xavier Hufkens 画廊首场个展时对我说。对特鲁韦而言，制图是一种相当奇妙的痴迷，因为她曾解释过，她是多么渴望体验那种迷失和“迷失方向”的感觉。", "links": [{"text": "Tatiana Trouvé", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/tatiana-trouve/"}, {"text": "Xavier Hufkens", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/xavier-hufkens/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "诸如此类的矛盾贯穿了这位艺术家的整个创作生涯。物件并非它们看上去的那样。装置模糊了档案记录与虚构之间的界限。然而，其姓氏在法语中极其巧合地意为“找到”的特鲁韦深信，“迷失是寻找自我的一种方式”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当你在某处迷路时，你会开始以不同的方式看待事物，”她继续说道，“你开始重建一条路径，不是你已经知道的那条，[而是]另一条能让你以不同方式被唤醒、找到自己的方向，并开始留意到那些当你确切知道如何从 A 点走到 B 点时根本不会注意的事物的路径。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特鲁韦的布鲁塞尔展览也是以同样的方式开场的。展期持续至 10月31日，涵盖了雕塑、素描和装置等多种形式，横跨画廊的全部3层。第一个展厅专门陈列《L’inventario》（2025），这是一种类似“库存”的作品，包含了她用金属和石头铸造的所有工作室材料，按类型和尺寸整齐排列，安装在以假乱真的青铜纸板架上。在这里，你会发现干花、用过的香皂、鞋子、包、泡沫垫、颜料瓶、书籍、纸质文件夹、发圈、打火机、被压扁的易拉罐、海盐贝、豆荚——列举不尽。虽然许多物品都可以在特鲁韦的工作室里找到，但也有许多实际上是凭空想象出来的。熟悉之物开始生出诡异之感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Linventario-2025-5.jpg?w=400", "alt": "由青铜和其他材质制成的雕塑，形似悬挂的干花、纸板架、水桶等。", "caption": "Tatiana Trouvé，《Inventario》，2025，布鲁塞尔 Xavier Hufkens 画廊展览现场。摄影：THOMAS MERLE/鸣谢艺术家与布鲁塞尔 Xavier Hufkens 画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "用黑色铸铁和石膏制作的一系列雕塑也是如此，它们是追踪巴黎市郊噪声污染的“图表”。这些黑色形态被抽象化，向下弯曲并伸向空中，似乎在挑战它们旨在测量的对象。它们遵循着一套我们无需完全理解的截然不同的冲动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当特鲁韦使用图表、地图或库存时，是为了将它们扭曲成新的形式。她在 1997 年至 2007 年间创作的突破性作品《Bureau d’Activités Implicites》（隐性活动局），呈现为一个虚构的办公装置，其中展示了诸如塞满了特鲁韦从未有过的经历的简历、成堆的求职被拒信、未实现的方案提案以及办公用品。Bureau 并没有成为一个旨在达成生产目标的办公空间，而是展示了沉思所花费的时间——既有漫无目的的，也有建设性的，而非一个最终的结果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特鲁韦似乎被任何暗示着某种秩序感的事物所吸引，并一路寻找着将其粉碎的方法。这种创作方式在她的素描中虽不那么显眼，却同样至关重要，这些素描具有某种宇宙学的维度。为了开始画画，特鲁韦将漂白剂倒在空白的工业彩色纸上。随着漂白剂在纸面上绽开、洗去纸浆中嵌入的染料，她开始“构建并寻找画作的路径”，将其发展为悬浮、重叠的星云状场景，其中自然与宇宙景观与室内建筑和几何平面相互碰撞。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我喜欢这种直面自己完全无法掌控的事物、必须展现出创造力和反思、并让自己完全被事物本身引导的过程，”她说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当被问及放弃如此多的控制权是否会让人感到害怕时，特鲁韦的脸上绽放出灿烂、青春的笑容。“这总是很难，但我想如果这一切都在我的控制之中，那对我来说就完全没有吸引力了，”她说，并补充说这也是她不以版本形式进行创作的原因。“把同一座雕塑做两遍对我来说深感无趣……唯一让我感兴趣的是，一件雕塑带给了我什么想法，以及对下一件雕塑的思考。事实上，我的作品永远关乎那些必须不断开启的大门。它是空间的延续。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Untitled-from-the-series-22Les-dessouvenus22-2024.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Tatiana Trouvé，《Untitled》，选自“Les dessouvenus”（被遗忘者）系列，2024。摄影：THOMAS MERLE/鸣谢艺术家与布鲁塞尔 Xavier Hufkens 画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在塞内加尔长大期间（她的家人于 1976 年从意大利搬到那里），特鲁韦开始从事艺术创作，并受到了吉姆（djinns，居住在花园里的隐形精灵）这一民间传说的影响。“我开始想象，或许我们才是幽灵，而不是它们，”她在 2005 年的一次采访中曾这样说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种魔幻现实般的思维延续到了她当前的实践中，这些创作既像是被隐形之躯所萦绕，又被我们自己活生生的呼吸所注入生机。那么，正如特鲁韦曾经想象的那样，我们是否已经变成了幽灵般的精灵？例如，她的《Sitting Sculptures》（2024–）正如标题所示，需要有人坐上去才能使其完整。它们由石头元素与泡沫垫和床垫的青铜铸件组合而成，这些材料支撑着特鲁韦的其他雕塑，但往往被忽视或变得“隐形”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在其中一件作品上小憩时，她谈到《Sitting Sculptures》时说：“它们不再支撑雕塑，而是支撑你。这里没有人形，但通过其缺席，人类在我的作品中无处不在。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sitting-Sculpture-2026.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Tatiana Trouvé，《Sitting Sculpture》，2026，布鲁塞尔 Xavier Hufkens 画廊展览现场。摄影：THOMAS MERLE/鸣谢艺术家与布鲁塞尔 Xavier Hufkens 画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "另一个例子体现在她广为人知的“守护者”（Guardian）系列（2013年至今）中，这是一组由浇铸石料和青铜制成的保安椅雕塑。部分灵感源自她曾担任博物馆保安的经历，它们通常伴有水瓶、靠垫、书籍或其他随身物品，给人一种坐在那里的人正在场的感觉。然而，保安本人并不在场。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在特鲁韦的叙述中，她的雕塑也注入了自身的感受甚至是期待。再上一层楼，当我们细看 L’inventario (2025) 的一小部分时，她指着一组带有莫兰迪风格的脏塑料瓶，其后挂着使用过的画笔、弄脏的调色板以及挤扁的油画颜料管。“这就像是一个渴望成为画作的小雕塑，”她说。“我认为物体有它们自己的生命。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在另一个角落，一件2026年的无题雕塑——由古铜色钢、涂漆铝、大理石、缟玛瑙和青铜制成，外形酷似带有衣架的衣帽架——看起来确实在霍夫肯斯画廊的布鲁塞尔空间里嬉戏了一番。在地板上，盘旋的笔触和痕迹似乎是用青铜衣帽架的金属脚在地画出的，仿佛它一路跳舞来到了现在的位置，留下了脚步的痕迹。它旁边是一个油漆桶，周围有更多的地面记号，神秘地通向一双从墙里伸出或走进墙里的黑色鞋子。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“通过它的运动，从某种意义上说，它在进行绘画，”特鲁韦谈到那个衣帽架时说道。如同一个移动的身体，这件装置“也让人想起一个不在场的人，这些没有身体的人物……这也某种程度上就像幽灵穿梭于我的作品中。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Untitled-2026-2.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一件由几个衣帽架和悬挂的石头衣架制成的青铜雕塑。", "caption": "塔蒂亚娜·特鲁韦（Tatiana Trouvé），《无题》（Untitled），2026年，展览现场，2026年，位于布鲁塞尔泽维尔·霍夫肯斯画廊（Xavier Hufkens）。图片：THOMAS MERLE / 致谢艺术家及布鲁塞尔泽维尔·霍夫肯斯画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I spend my time making maps,” Tatiana Trouvé told me as we ambled through her first exhibition with Brussels-based gallery Xavier Hufkens . Map-making is a rather curious obsession for Trouvé to have, given how keenly she wants to experience the feeling of being lost and “disoriented,” she explained.", "links": [{"text": "Tatiana Trouvé", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/tatiana-trouve/"}, {"text": "Xavier Hufkens", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/xavier-hufkens/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Contradictions like these are a hallmark across the artist’s oeuvre. Objects aren’t quite what they appear to be. Installations blur the line between archival documentation and fiction. But Trouvé, whose last name, incredibly, means “found” in French, believes that “being lost is a way of finding oneself.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When you get lost somewhere, you start looking at things differently,” she continued. “You begin rebuilding a path, not the way you already know, [but] something else that allows you to feel awakened in a different way, to navigate your way and become attuned to things you don’t notice when you know exactly how to get from A to B.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Trouvé’s Brussels exhibition begins in much the same way. On view through October 31, it features a mix of sculptures, drawings, and installations and spans all three of the gallery’s floors. The first room is devoted to L’inventario (2025), an “inventory” of sorts that contains all her studio materials cast in metal and stone, arranged in neat rows by type and size, installed atop convincingly illusionistic cardboard shelves made of bronze. Here, you’ll find dried flowers, used soaps, shoes, bags, foam padding, paint bottles, books, paper folders, scrunchies, lighters, flattened soda cans, seashells, pea pods—the list goes on. While many of the items can be found in Trouvé’s studio, many are actually imagined. The familiar begins to feel uncanny."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Linventario-2025-5.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Sculptures made of bronze and other materials that resemble hanging dried flowers, cardboard shelves, buckets, and more. ", "caption": "Tatiana Trouvé, Inventario , 2025, installation view, at Xavier Hufkens, Brussels. Photo THOMAS MERLE/Courtesy the artist and Xavier Hufkens, Brussels", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That is also the case with a series of sculptures made with black cast iron and plaster that are “diagrams” tracking noise pollution on the outskirts of Paris. Rendered abstract, these black forms curl down and reach into the air, seeming to defy what they purport to measure. They adhere to an entirely different set of impulses we need not fully understand."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When Trouvé works with diagrams, maps, or inventories, it is to distort them into new forms. Her breakthrough work Bureau d’Activités Implicites (Bureau of Implicit Activities) , developed between 1997 and 2007, took the shape of a fictional office installation that displayed things like résumés packed with experiences Trouvé has never had, piles of job rejection letters, unrealized project proposals, and office supplies. Instead of being a workspace designed to meet production goals, Bureau was a display of time spent thinking, both listless and constructive, rather than a final result."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Trouvé seems drawn to anything that implies a semblance of order and finding ways of shattering it along the way. article_text:
“I spend my time making maps,” Tatiana Trouvé told me as we ambled through her first exhibition with Brussels-based gallery Xavier Hufkens . Map-making is a rather curious obsession for Trouvé to have, given how keenly she wants to experience the feeling of being lost and “disoriented,” she explained.

Contradictions like these are a hallmark across the artist’s oeuvre. Objects aren’t quite what they appear to be. Installations blur the line between archival documentation and fiction. But Trouvé, whose last name, incredibly, means “found” in French, believes that “being lost is a way of finding oneself.”

“When you get lost somewhere, you start looking at things differently,” she continued. “You begin rebuilding a path, not the way you already know, [but] something else that allows you to feel awakened in a different way, to navigate your way and become attuned to things you don’t notice when you know exactly how to get from A to B.”

Trouvé’s Brussels exhibition begins in much the same way. On view through October 31, it features a mix of sculptures, drawings, and installations and spans all three of the gallery’s floors. The first room is devoted to L’inventario (2025), an “inventory” of sorts that contains all her studio materials cast in metal and stone, arranged in neat rows by type and size, installed atop convincingly illusionistic cardboard shelves made of bronze. Here, you’ll find dried flowers, used soaps, shoes, bags, foam padding, paint bottles, books, paper folders, scrunchies, lighters, flattened soda cans, seashells, pea pods—the list goes on. While many of the items can be found in Trouvé’s studio, many are actually imagined. The familiar begins to feel uncanny.

That is also the case with a series of sculptures made with black cast iron and plaster that are “diagrams” tracking noise pollution on the outskirts of Paris. Rendered abstract, these black forms curl down and reach into the air, seeming to defy what they purport to measure. They adhere to an entirely different set of impulses we need not fully understand.

When Trouvé works with diagrams, maps, or inventories, it is to distort them into new forms. Her breakthrough work Bureau d’Activités Implicites (Bureau of Implicit Activities) , developed between 1997 and 2007, took the shape of a fictional office installation that displayed things like résumés packed with experiences Trouvé has never had, piles of job rejection letters, unrealized project proposals, and office supplies. Instead of being a workspace designed to meet production goals, Bureau was a display of time spent thinking, both listless and constructive, rather than a final result.

Trouvé seems drawn to anything that implies a semblance of order and finding ways of shattering it along the way. That way of working is less obvious but just as essential in her drawings, which have a cosmological dimension to them. To begin her drawings, Trouvé pours bleach onto blank sheets of industrial colored paper. As the bleach blooms across the surface, removing the dyes embedded in the pulp, she starts to “build and find the drawing’s path,” developing them into floating, overlapping nebulae-like scenes, where natural and cosmic landscapes butt against architectural interiors and geometric planes.

“I like this process of being confronted with something I have absolutely no mastery over, where I have to show inventiveness and reflection, and let myself be completely guided by the things themselves,” she said.

When asked if it can be frightening to abandon so much control, Trouvé’s face lit up with a wide, youthful smile. “It’s always hard, but I think there would be no interest left for me at all if I had control over all of this,” she said, adding that she doesn’t work in editions for that reason. “Doing the same sculpture twice is profoundly boring to me. … The only thing that interests me is what idea a sculpture has given me, what thoughts for the next one. In fact, my work is always about doors that must continuously open. It’s a continuation of spaces.”

While growing up in Senegal, where her family moved in 1976 from Italy, Trouvé began making art and was influenced by the folkloric tradition of djinns, invisible spirits who live in gardens. “I started imagining that perhaps we, not they, were the ghosts,” she has said in a 2005 interview.

This magical thinking has extended into her current practice, which can feel both haunted by invisible bodies and animated by our own living and breathing ones. Have we, then, become the ghostly spirits, as Trouvé once imagined? Her Sitting Sculptures (2024–), for instance, are meant to be sat upon, as the title suggests, as a way to complete them. They are made of stone elements combined with bronze casts of foam padding and mattresses, materials that support Trouvé’s other sculptures but are often disregarded or rendered “invisible.”

“They no longer support the sculpture, but they support you,” she said of the Sitting Sculptures , while we took a break on one of them. “There are no human figures, but the human is ever-present in my work, through its absence,” Trouvé said.

Another example of this is in her well-known “Guardian” series (2013–) of cast stone and bronze sculptures of security-guard chairs. Partly inspired by her time working as a museum security guard, they are often accompanied by water bottles, cushions, books, or other belongings that give a sense of the presence of the person who sits there. The guard, however, is absent.

In Trouvé’s telling, her sculptures are also imbued with their own feelings and even expectations. One floor up, as we inspect a small part of L’inventario (2025), she pointed to an arrangement of dirtied, Morandi-like plastic bottles, behind which hang used brushes, dirtied paint pallets and squeezed-out tubes of oil paint. “This is like a little sculpture that dreams of being a painting,” she said. “I think objects have a life of their own.”

Elsewhere, a 2026 untitled sculpture—made of patinated steel, painted aluminum, marble, onyx, and bronze and resembling a coat rack with hangers—certainly seems to have spent some time frolicking in Hufkens’s Brussels gallery. On the floor, twirling strokes and marks appear to have been made on the ground using the metallic feet of the bronze coat rack, as if it has danced its way to its current location, leaving behind traces of its steps. Beside it is a bucket of paint surrounded by more floor markings leading mysteriously to a pair of black shoes coming out of or going into the wall.

“Through her movement, in a sense, she is drawing,” Trouvé said of the coat rack. Like a moving body, the installation “also recalls a person who is not there, these figures without bodies. … It is also somewhat like ghosts passing through my work.”

article_text:
New York Newsletter

NYC Artists Open Their Doors

Open studios and houses, plus reviews of Betty Parsons, Riddikuluz, and the L train burlesque.

I was way too productive throughout the three-day weekend. A grueling closet overhaul (five-drawer wooden tallboy vs. fourth-floor walk-up), an overdue bathroom bleachout, a close friend’s 30th birthday party, a drop-in cat-sitting visit that turned into a rare accidental nap, and an arduous round-trip trek to the distant land of Nassau County were accomplished, and yet I still feel haplessly behind on my never-ending to-do list.

Looking at the upcoming roster for the rest of the month, I’m positive that I’m not the only one who’ll be letting that to-do list pile up again in favor of ✨ immersing myself in the culture ✨. Much like my closet door for the better part of the last eight months, the doors to New York City are going to be wide open this weekend. Sunset Park and Gowanus are hosting their annual open studios, which happen to coincide with the broader Open House New York (OHNY) weekend programming. We’ve highlighted a selection of intriguing OHNY happenings at the bottom of this newsletter! :)

In observance of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we highlighted a wealth of Native American art happenings across the city and state. Take a look at our round-up of seven exhibitions embodying Indigenous survivance and Associate Editor Phillip Pyle’s rich Q&A with Diné artist and composer Raven Chacon, who recently led an hour-long improvisational sound performance at the Park Avenue Armory last week. In the same vein, Staff Writer Anna Lee reported that the Gochman Family Collection is set to open its Katonah site for exhibiting contemporary Indigenous art next month!

Remember last week’s newsletter, when I mentioned that the Department of Cultural Affairs announced that city-funded artists' grants jumped from $5,000 to $10,000? Well, an additional perk has been revealed: starting October 19, those who are afforded grants will also gain access to the city’s beloved Materials for the Arts warehouse on the second Monday of each month. Congratulations in advance to those who will deservedly reap these benefits!

Happy reading, and I’ll see you at the Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade!

7 New York Exhibitions That Embody Indigenous Survivance

To commemorate Indigenous Peoples’ Day here in New York, we highlighted seven ongoing exhibitions of Native art and history in Manhattan, the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College, and the Long Island Museum in Stony Brook. Across solo and group presentations, the featured artists, who represent a diverse tapestry of Indigenous populations across Turtle Island, embody survivance by tracing and rejecting narratives of dispossession and irrelevance, upending and satirizing stereotypes, preserving and reinventing traditional art forms, and bringing underrepresented histories out from the margins. | Rhea Nayyar

Read More

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.” | Phillip Pyle

Read More

Quilt Along: Sit and Sew at the National Museum of the American Indian

Meet artist Margaret Wood (Diné/Seminole), one of five contemporary Indigenous artists featured in the museum’s first-ever Quilt Along program. The artists designed patterns inspired by different eras of United States history, as seen through a Native lens.

Learn more and join us Saturday, October 17, 1–3 PM.

Register Now

From Our Critics

Hrag Vartanian

Pleasure Dome: Continuum at SoMad

"The gathering became a fête of therapeutic sound, queer political rally, vaudeville tribute, and a vibe manifesto for a city that is constantly shattering the old to make way for the new."

Daniel Larkin

KLAB at Salma Sarriedine gallery

"In Ridikkuluz’s work, the irascible dog emerges as a symbol for the ongoing genocide and its unrestrained perpetrators."

Julia Curl

settle for a good fantasy at Luhring Augustine

"In one set of eight prints, the artist rubs dark makeup from her eyes, a gesture reminiscent of crying. As her eyeshadow smears, it leaves what look like bruises, creating a dissonant, double feeling of pain and pleasure — and the acknowledgment that it’s all just an act."

Seph Rodney

Betty Parsons: An Expanded World at the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College

"Regardless of the aesthetic merit or caliber of the work, this artist, like any other, deserves to have her own space free of another artist’s intervention because she is well able to stand on her own two feet."

A Hyperallergic Halloween

Join us on October 28 in Brooklyn, NY, for an evening of spooky cocktails, devilish delights, an art-themed costume contest, and more.

Learn more and Get Tickets

News

After a five-year pause, the New Museum in Manhattan will open its sixth triennial for emerging artists in early 2027.

Materials for the Arts is launching a new free shopping program for artists who receive city-funded grants.

The Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art is opening a space in Katonah this November.

Over two dozen people assembled down the street from the Museum of Modern Art calling for the removal of disgraced billionaire Leon Black from the museum board.

What Else Is Happening?

Sunset Park Open Studios is this weekend! (Fri Oct 16 through Sun Oct 18) [ sunsetparkopenstudios.org ]

Print Center New York is hosting a rubber stamp workshop. (Sat Oct 17) [ printcenternewyork.org ]

The Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade returns this Saturday for its 36th edition. (Sat Oct 17) [ nydogparade.org ]

Pioneers in Hand Papermaking commemorates 50 years of NYC’s fine arts papermill, Dieu Donné, with a display of over 100 artworks and material innovations. (Sat Oct 17) [ OHNY.org ]

Tom's Sons, a diasporic Armenian family-owned textile pleating business in the Garment District, explains their generationally perfected craft. (Sat Oct 17) [ OHNY.org ]

The New York Sign Museum invites visitors to check out its collection of preserved hand-painted and craft signage embodying different eras of design thinking throughout the 20th century. (Sat Oct 17 and and Sun Oct 18) [ OHNY.org ]

Gowanus Open Studios is this weekend! (Sat Oct 17 through Sun Oct 18) [ artsgowanus.org ]

Palestine Will Be Free: The Story of Hanzala is a concert built around 100 of Palestinian cartoonist Naji al-Ali's drawings, animated and projected above a nine-piece ensemble playing twelve songs of childhood, freedom, and return. (Sun Oct 18) [ thebrooklynnomads.com ]

Slo Slo Studio is hosting a handmade ceramic bookends workshop. (Sun Oct 18) [ sloslostudio.kilnfire.com ]

The Center for Book Arts is hosting live demonstrations of historic and contemporary bookmaking steps and techniques, including letterpress printing to sewing frames. (Sun., Oct 18) [ OHNY.org ]

Rizzoli Bookstore celebrates the new monograph, Brilliant: Unexpected Art from Everywhere , with a conversation between Roxane Gay and her wife, Debbie Millman. (Mon Oct 19) [ Rizzoli Bookstore ]

AI Now Institute and More Perfect Union are leading the People's AI Assembly, an evening bringing together leading organizers, cultural figures, and policy leaders shaping the frontlines of AI. (Mon Oct 19) [ actionnetwork.org ]
